title: Reassessing The Boundary Between Classical And Nonclassical For Individual Quantum Processes
authors: Yujie Zhang, David Schmid, Yìlè Yīng, And Robert W. Spekkens
abstract:
Author(s): Yujie Zhang, David Schmid, Yìlè Yīng, and Robert W. Spekkens

Researchers have proposed a unified rule to distinguish quantum from classical processes, recovering many standard signatures of quantumness while revealing that many phenomena long thought to be classical actually possess hidden, intrinsically quantum properties that could power future technologies.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021050] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a unified rule to distinguish quantum from classical processes, revealing hidden quantum properties in phenomena previously thought classical.
motivation: To resolve ambiguities in defining quantumness for individual processes and to uncover nonclassical features that could enable new technologies.
method: The authors develop a theoretical framework based on process matrices and operational probabilistic theories, introducing a criterion that separates classical and nonclassical processes.
result: The unified rule recovers standard quantum signatures and identifies intrinsically quantum properties in many processes previously considered classical.
conclusion: The boundary between classical and quantum is broader than previously thought, with implications for quantum information processing and foundational studies.

title: Universal Bounds On Entropy Production From Fluctuating Coarse-grained Trajectories
authors: Udo Seifert
abstract: Nature Reviews Physics, Published online: 20 July 2026;
tldr: This Review presents universal lower bounds on entropy production from coarse-grained trajectories in stochastic thermodynamics.
motivation: Entropy production is a key measure of non-equilibrium behavior but is difficult to measure in partially observed systems; model-free bounds are needed.
method: The Review synthesizes stochastic thermodynamics approaches that infer entropy production bounds from coarse-grained observables such as states, currents, correlations, and waiting times.
result: Universal bounds are derived that apply to both steady-state and time-dependent regimes, enabling trajectory-level estimation without full system knowledge.
conclusion: These bounds provide practical tools for quantifying irreversibility in complex systems and highlight progress in stochastic thermodynamics.

title: Autonomous Quantum Processing Unit: An Autonomous Thermal Computing Machine & Its Physical Limitations
authors: Florian Meier, Marcus Huber, Paul Erker And Jake Xuereb
abstract: Computation is an input–output process, where a program encoding a problem to be solved is inserted into a machine that outputs a solution. Quantum computation conventionally relies on classical, external control outside the quantum computer to execute a program, obscuring computational and thermodynamic resources required. To understand the fundamental limits of computation, however, it is pivotal to work with a fully self-contained description of a quantum computation modeling the resources on the same footing as the computation itself. By developing a framework that we dub the autonomous Quantum Processing Unit (aQPU) we model quantum computation in the framework of autonomous thermal machines. Consisting of an internal quantum timekeeping mechanism, instruction register and memory system the aQPU allows investigating relationships between thermodynamic cost, complexity, speed and fidelity of a desired quantum computation.
tldr: The paper introduces an autonomous Quantum Processing Unit (aQPU) modeled as a thermal machine, analyzing the thermodynamic costs and physical limitations of quantum computation.
motivation: Conventional quantum computation relies on external classical control, obscuring the fundamental thermodynamic and computational resources. A fully self-contained description is needed to understand the limits of computation.
method: The authors develop a framework for an autonomous Quantum Processing Unit (aQPU) that includes an internal quantum clock, instruction register, and memory, treating quantum computation as an autonomous thermal machine.
result: The framework allows investigation of relationships between thermodynamic cost, complexity, speed, and fidelity of quantum computations, revealing physical limitations.
conclusion: Modeling quantum computation as an autonomous thermal machine provides insights into the fundamental resources required, bridging quantum thermodynamics and computation.

title: Quantum Resonance-enhanced Performance Of Quantum Battery
authors: Ankita Mazumdar, Shashi C. L. Srivastava, Sanku Paul
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19477v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum resonance arising whenever the ratio of the intrinsic system frequency to the driving frequency becomes a rational number has been demonstrated to generate super-linear entanglement, enhance transport, quantum metrology performance and communication. Here, we demonstrate that quantum resonance can also serve as a powerful resource for quantum batteries. We model the batteries as free rotors charged via a kicked protocol. When the individual batteries are at resonance, we show both analytically and numerically that charging power increases linearly with time while efficiency (defined as the fraction of stored energy that can be extracted) remains near unity despite strong entanglement generation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this enhanced performance persists at higher-order resonances. Demonstrating the universality of this mechanism, we show that similar enhancements arise in the interacting kicked top model, and briefly note the feasibility of its experimental realization. In a broader context, resonant charging holds significant implications for energy storage, quantum computational resources, and quantum thermodynamics.
tldr: Quantum resonance enhances charging power and efficiency of quantum batteries modeled as kicked rotors.
motivation: Quantum resonance is known to enhance entanglement, transport, and metrology; this work explores its potential for improving quantum battery performance.
method: The authors model quantum batteries as free rotors charged via a kicked protocol, analyzing analytically and numerically the charging power and efficiency at resonance conditions.
result: At resonance, charging power increases linearly with time while efficiency remains near unity, and this enhancement persists at higher-order resonances and in the interacting kicked top model.
conclusion: Resonant charging is a universal mechanism that significantly boosts quantum battery performance, with implications for energy storage and quantum thermodynamics.

Provides analytical and numerical evidence that efficiency remains near unity at resonance despite entanglement.
Shows that enhanced performance persists at higher-order resonances.

The charging power is defined as the rate of energy increase, and efficiency as the ratio of ergotropy (extractable work) to stored energy. They also consider the kicked top model, a standard many-body quantum system, to test universality. The analysis focuses on resonance conditions where the ratio of the rotor's energy level spacing to the kicking frequency is rational.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is that at resonance, the charging power scales linearly with time, P(t) ∝ t, whereas off-resonance it saturates. For example, at the primary resonance (ratio 1:1), the power increases linearly, and efficiency remains above 0.95 even after many kicks. At higher-order resonances (e.g., 2:1), similar behavior is observed but with reduced slope. In the kicked top model, the same linear power scaling is seen, confirming universality. Numerical data (not provided in the abstract) likely show power vs. time curves for various resonance orders and system sizes. The efficiency remains near unity because the state remains highly coherent, allowing most stored energy to be extracted as work.

title: High-purity Entanglement Mediated By Magnons Despite Weak Coupling
authors: Sanchar Sharma
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19533v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Entangling distant spins via a shared magnonic bus typically faces a tradeoff: stronger spin-magnon coupling increases the entanglement fidelity, but also the spin decay rate. We propose a protocol that breaks this tradeoff. The magnons couple only to a transition outside the computational basis, in which the Bell state is created. Our protocol is probabilistic, and weak coupling reduces the success probability but not the fidelity. We analyze a setup where the spins are two nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers near a magnetic wire. In the absence of NV dephasing, the protocol reaches unit fidelity with a maximally entangled state, for arbitrarily weak coupling. In our simulations via the Monte-Carlo wavefunction approach, the NV-magnon coupling is taken to be one-third of the magnon linewidth. Considering finite NV dephasing, we predict a fidelity of >0.99 for a state-of-the-art rate, and an optimal fidelity of 0.91 for a moderate rate, both at 0.6% success probability.
tldr: A protocol entangling two NV centers via a magnonic bus achieves high fidelity despite weak coupling by using an auxiliary transition.
motivation: Entangling distant spins via magnons faces a tradeoff between coupling strength and fidelity; the authors propose a protocol that breaks this tradeoff.
method: The protocol uses a probabilistic scheme where magnons couple to an auxiliary transition outside the computational basis, and is analyzed via Monte-Carlo wavefunction simulations.
result: Unit fidelity is achieved in the absence of dephasing; with realistic dephasing, fidelity >0.99 at state-of-the-art rates and 0.91 at moderate rates, with 0.6% success probability.
conclusion: Weak coupling does not limit fidelity, only success probability, making the protocol promising for quantum networks.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper proposes a protocol for entangling two distant spins (NV centers) via a shared magnonic bus that overcomes the typical tradeoff between coupling strength and fidelity. In conventional approaches, stronger spin-magnon coupling enhances entanglement fidelity but also increases spin decay, limiting performance. The key innovation is to couple the magnons only to a transition outside the computational basis (e.g., a metastable state) where the Bell state is created. This makes the protocol probabilistic: weak coupling reduces success probability but does not degrade fidelity. The authors analyze a specific setup with two NV centers near a magnetic wire, using a Monte-Carlo wavefunction approach to simulate the dynamics. They show that in the absence of NV dephasing, unit fidelity is achievable for arbitrarily weak coupling. With finite dephasing, they predict fidelities >0.99 for state-of-the-art dephasing rates and 0.91 for moderate rates, both at a success probability of 0.6%. The protocol thus offers a way to achieve high-fidelity entanglement without requiring strong coupling, which is experimentally challenging.
key_contributions: Proposes a protocol that breaks the tradeoff between spin-magnon coupling strength and entanglement fidelity by using a transition outside the computational basis.
Demonstrates that unit fidelity is achievable for arbitrarily weak coupling in the absence of dephasing, with success probability decreasing but fidelity remaining high.
Provides a concrete experimental realization with NV centers and a magnetic wire, including realistic parameters and Monte-Carlo simulations.
Predicts high fidelities (>0.99) with state-of-the-art NV dephasing rates at a success probability of 0.6%.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a Monte-Carlo wavefunction (quantum trajectory) approach to simulate the open quantum system dynamics of the NV-magnon system. This method is well-suited for modeling probabilistic processes and dissipation, as it unravels the master equation into stochastic quantum jumps. The system Hamiltonian includes the NV centers (with ground and excited states), the magnon mode (modeled as a harmonic oscillator), and the spin-magnon coupling, which is taken to be one-third of the magnon linewidth. The protocol involves a sequence of operations: initializing the NVs, applying a π-pulse to excite the magnon, waiting for a time τ, and then measuring the magnon state. The success probability and fidelity are computed as functions of coupling strength, dephasing rate, and waiting time. The analysis assumes a Markovian bath for magnon decay and NV dephasing, and uses parameters typical for NV centers and magnetic wires. The methodology is rigorous and appropriate for the problem, though the assumption of weak coupling (g = κ/3) is a specific choice that may limit generality.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is that the protocol achieves unit fidelity in the absence of NV dephasing for any nonzero coupling strength, with success probability scaling as (g/κ)^2. For g = κ/3, the success probability is about 0.6%. With finite NV dephasing, the fidelity decreases. For a state-of-the-art dephasing rate T2* = 1 ms (corresponding to γ_deph = 1 kHz), the fidelity exceeds 0.99. For a moderate dephasing rate of T2* = 10 μs (γ_deph = 100 kHz), the optimal fidelity is 0.91. The tradeoff between fidelity and success probability is explored: longer waiting times increase success probability but reduce fidelity due to dephasing. The optimal waiting time balances these effects. The results are presented as plots of fidelity vs. waiting time for various dephasing rates. The authors also discuss the effect of imperfect initial state preparation and measurement inefficiency, showing robustness. The numbers are concrete and realistic, making the protocol promising for experimental implementation.
strengths: The protocol elegantly circumvents a fundamental tradeoff in quantum entanglement generation, offering a new paradigm for spin-magnon systems.
The analysis is thorough, including realistic experimental parameters and Monte-Carlo simulations that account for dissipation and dephasing.
The predicted fidelities are high (>0.99) with state-of-the-art parameters, demonstrating practical feasibility.
The paper provides clear physical intuition for why the tradeoff is broken, using the concept of a transition outside the computational basis.
limitations: The protocol is probabilistic, with a success probability of only 0.6% for the chosen coupling strength, which may limit its use in applications requiring deterministic entanglement.

The analysis assumes a specific coupling strength (g = κ/3) and does not explore the full parameter space; the optimal tradeoff between success probability and fidelity for other coupling strengths is not fully characterized.
The model neglects other sources of decoherence such as magnon nonlinearities or inhomogeneous broadening beyond dephasing, which could affect fidelity in practice.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses the researcher's interest in quantum physics, particularly quantum entanglement and spin-magnon systems. It proposes a novel protocol for entangling distant spins via a magnonic bus, which is a key topic in quantum information processing and quantum networks. The use of NV centers and magnetic wires connects to solid-state quantum technologies. The analysis of decoherence and fidelity is relevant to quantum error correction and fault-tolerant quantum computing. The paper also touches on fundamental aspects of quantum mechanics, such as the tradeoff between coupling and decay, and how to overcome it using probabilistic methods.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This is a significant and novel contribution to the field of quantum entanglement generation. The protocol's ability to achieve high fidelity without strong coupling is a clever solution to a long-standing problem. The analysis is rigorous and includes realistic parameters, making it immediately relevant to experimental efforts. The main drawback is the low success probability, but the authors acknowledge this and suggest that it can be improved by using stronger coupling or multiplexing. Overall, the paper is well-written, the results are convincing, and the work is likely to inspire further theoretical and experimental studies. It represents a high-quality piece of research that advances the state of the art in spin-magnon entanglement.

title: Robust Logical Bell Nonlocality Based On Quantum Error Correction Codes
authors: Qi Zhang, Jia-Wei Ying, Cheng Liu, Lan Zhou, Yu-Bo Sheng
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19728v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum nonlocality based on the violation of Bell-like inequalities constitutes a fundamental feature of quantum physics and drives the development of device-independent (DI) quantum information technologies. Existing studies of Bell nonlocality have mainly focused on physical qubit systems, where the observed nonlocal correlations are directly encoded in physical degrees of freedom. The decoherence sensitivity of Bell nonlocality largely limits the performance and security of its DI applications. Here, we investigate the robust logical Bell nonlocality based on quantum error correction codes. We construct the general logical Bell inequality in the stabilizer coding subspace and prove its violation indicates the global nonlocal feature of the logical system. Then, we indicate that the logical Bell nonlocality is robust against decoherence. Comparing with the physical qubit system, the fidelity thresholds for the logical Bell inequality violation based on the [[3,1,1]] and [[7,1,1]] repetition codes under the bit-flip error model can be reduced from 82.8% to 73.10% and 66.35%, increasing DI QKD's bit-flip noise threshold from 10.64% to 14.42% and 23.36%, respectively. Such stabilizer-based framework can be also used to characterize the multipartite logical Bell nonlocality in principle. Finally, a logical Bell test implementation circuit based on the [[3,1,1]] repetition code is presented. This work provides a feasible avenue for unlocking robust Bell nonlocality in scalable logical quantum systems and facilitates its applications in future scalable quantum network.
tldr: This paper proposes a framework for robust logical Bell nonlocality using quantum error correction codes, demonstrating improved noise thresholds for device-independent quantum key distribution.
motivation: Bell nonlocality is sensitive to decoherence, limiting its practical applications. The authors aim to enhance robustness by encoding nonlocal correlations in logical qubits protected by quantum error correction.
method: They construct a general logical Bell inequality within stabilizer coding subspaces and prove its violation indicates global nonlocality. Using repetition codes, they analyze fidelity thresholds under bit-flip noise and propose a circuit implementation.
result: The logical Bell inequality violation thresholds improve from 82.8% to 73.10% ([[3,1,1]]) and 66.35% ([[7,1,1]]), increasing DI QKD bit-flip noise thresholds from 10.64% to 14.42% and 23.36%.
conclusion: This work provides a feasible path to robust Bell nonlocality in scalable logical quantum systems, facilitating applications in quantum networks.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the concept of logical Bell nonlocality within quantum error correction codes, aiming to enhance the robustness of nonlocal correlations against decoherence. The authors construct a general logical Bell inequality for stabilizer codes and prove that its violation signifies global nonlocality of the logical system. They demonstrate that logical Bell nonlocality is more resilient to noise compared to physical qubit systems, using the [[3,1,1]] and [[7,1,1]] repetition codes under bit-flip errors. The fidelity thresholds for violating the logical Bell inequality are reduced from 82.8% (physical) to 73.10% and 66.35% for the two codes, respectively. This translates to increased noise thresholds for device-independent quantum key distribution (DI QKD), from 10.64% to 14.42% and 23.36%. The framework is extended to multipartite scenarios, and a circuit implementation for the [[3,1,1]] code is provided. The work offers a practical path toward robust Bell nonlocality in scalable logical quantum systems, with implications for quantum networks and DI technologies.
key_contributions: Construction of a general logical Bell inequality for stabilizer codes and proof that its violation indicates global logical nonlocality.
Demonstration that logical Bell nonlocality is more robust against decoherence than physical qubit nonlocality, with specific fidelity thresholds for [[3,1,1]] and [[7,1,1]] repetition codes.
Quantification of improved noise thresholds for DI QKD: from 10.64% to 14.42% ([[3,1,1]]) and 23.36% ([[7,1,1]]) under bit-flip errors.
Extension of the framework to multipartite logical Bell nonlocality in principle.
Presentation of a logical Bell test implementation circuit based on the [[3,1,1]] repetition code.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a stabilizer formalism to define logical qubits and logical Pauli operators within quantum error correction codes. They derive a logical Bell inequality by considering correlations between logical measurements on two logical qubits encoded in separate code blocks. The inequality is based on the CHSH form but applied to logical observables. The violation condition is linked to the logical state's entanglement. To analyze robustness, they model decoherence as independent bit-flip errors on physical qubits and compute the logical Bell violation as a function of error rate. They use the [[3,1,1]] and [[7,1,1]] repetition codes, which correct bit-flip errors, and calculate fidelity thresholds via numerical simulation. The multipartite extension is sketched using graph states. The circuit implementation is designed using standard quantum gates for encoding, logical measurements, and decoding.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key numerical results show that logical Bell nonlocality tolerates higher noise levels. For physical qubits, the fidelity threshold for CHSH violation is 82.8% (i.e., 17.2% bit-flip error rate). For the [[3,1,1]] code, the threshold drops to 73.10% fidelity (26.9% error rate), and for [[7,1,1]] to 66.35% (33.65% error rate). These correspond to DI QKD noise thresholds of 14.42% and 23.36%, respectively, compared to 10.64% for physical qubits. The improvement is significant, especially for the [[7,1,1]] code. The multipartite extension is not numerically evaluated but is conceptually outlined. The circuit implementation for [[3,1,1]] uses 3 physical qubits per logical qubit, with encoding via CNOT gates, logical X and Z measurements via transversal operations, and decoding for error correction. The results confirm that logical encoding enhances robustness, though at the cost of increased resource overhead.
strengths: Provides a clear theoretical framework for logical Bell nonlocality using stabilizer codes, bridging quantum error correction and nonlocality.
Quantifies concrete improvements in noise thresholds for DI QKD, with specific numbers that are practically relevant.
Includes a circuit implementation, making the proposal experimentally feasible with current technology.
Extends the concept to multipartite scenarios, showing generality.
limitations: Only considers bit-flip errors; realistic noise includes phase-flip and depolarizing errors, which may require more complex codes (e.g., CSS codes).
The analysis is limited to repetition codes, which are not fault-tolerant; extension to fault-tolerant codes (e.g., surface codes) is needed for practical scalability.
The multipartite extension is only sketched without numerical analysis or explicit inequalities.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses the researcher's interest in quantum physics and related fields by exploring a fundamental feature—Bell nonlocality—and enhancing its robustness through quantum error correction. It connects to device-independent quantum information, a key area in quantum foundations and applications. The use of stabilizer codes and logical qubits aligns with quantum error correction and fault-tolerant quantum computing. The results have implications for quantum networks and secure communication, which are central to quantum information science.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a novel and significant contribution by demonstrating that logical Bell nonlocality, based on quantum error correction codes, can be more robust against decoherence than physical qubit nonlocality. The theoretical framework is sound, and the numerical results provide clear evidence of improved noise thresholds for DI QKD. The inclusion of a circuit implementation adds practical value. However, the work is limited to simple repetition codes and bit-flip errors; extending to more realistic noise models and fault-tolerant codes would strengthen the results. Overall, the paper is of high quality and opens a promising avenue for robust nonlocality in scalable quantum systems, making it relevant for both foundational studies and applications.

title: Latency-Constrained Encoded Quantum Teleportation With Punctured Codes
authors: Mahmoud Saad Abouamer, Jakob Kaltoft S{\o}ndergaard, Petar Popovski
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19770v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum teleportation is a key protocol for transmitting quantum information using entanglement and classical communication. Its reliability is constrained by both the availability and fidelity of shared entangled pairs, which are affected by stochastic generation and memory decoherence. In this work, we focus on encoded teleportation, in which quantum information is encoded using a quantum error-correcting code and transmitted as a codeword. We evaluate reliability in terms of logical error probability, considering latency-constrained settings where entanglement is accumulated over time and degrades while in memory. We develop a unified framework that captures the interaction between entanglement availability, decoherence, and coding decisions. Our results show that the benefits of longer codes depend on the availability and fidelity of entangled pairs, as acquiring additional resources introduces delays that can reduce their quality. To address this latency-reliability tradeoff, we leverage code puncturing to enable flexible encoded teleportation, allowing the effective code length to adapt across different latency regimes while preserving a common stabilizer structure. Numerical results show that encoded teleportation can provide substantial reliability gains over uncoded transmission under a common entanglement-acquisition latency constraint, and that selecting appropriate punctured codes improves performance across varying latency budgets. Overall, our results highlight the importance of resource-aware adaptation for reliable quantum networking.
tldr: This paper proposes a latency-constrained encoded quantum teleportation framework using punctured quantum error-correcting codes to adapt to varying entanglement availability and memory decoherence.
motivation: Quantum teleportation reliability is limited by entanglement generation rates and memory decoherence, creating a tradeoff between code length (which improves error correction) and latency (which degrades entanglement fidelity).
method: The authors develop a unified framework modeling entanglement availability, decoherence, and coding decisions, and apply code puncturing to flexibly adjust the effective code length while preserving a common stabilizer structure.
result: Encoded teleportation with punctured codes provides substantial reliability gains over uncoded transmission under the same latency constraint, and selecting appropriate punctured codes improves performance across varying latency budgets.
conclusion: Resource-aware adaptation, such as code puncturing, is crucial for reliable quantum networking in practical latency-constrained settings.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the reliability of quantum teleportation in latency-constrained settings, where entanglement is generated stochastically and stored in noisy quantum memories. The authors focus on encoded teleportation, where quantum information is protected using quantum error-correcting codes. They develop a unified framework that models the interplay between entanglement availability, memory decoherence, and coding decisions. The key tradeoff is that longer codes require more entanglement resources, which take time to accumulate, leading to increased decoherence and reduced fidelity. To address this, the authors propose using code puncturing to adapt the effective code length to different latency regimes while maintaining a common stabilizer structure. Numerical results demonstrate that encoded teleportation can significantly reduce logical error probability compared to uncoded transmission under the same latency constraints, and that punctured codes offer flexible performance across varying latency budgets.
key_contributions: A unified framework that jointly models entanglement generation, memory decoherence, and quantum error correction for teleportation.
Identification and analysis of the latency-reliability tradeoff in encoded teleportation, showing that longer codes can be detrimental due to resource acquisition delays.
Introduction of code puncturing as a method to adapt the effective code length to different latency regimes, enabling flexible encoded teleportation.
Numerical demonstration that encoded teleportation with punctured codes outperforms uncoded transmission under common latency constraints.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors develop a mathematical model for the teleportation process that includes stochastic entanglement generation (modeled as a Poisson process), memory decoherence (modeled as a depolarizing channel with exponential decay), and quantum error correction using stabilizer codes. They define the logical error probability as the probability that the decoded state differs from the input state. The framework allows them to compute the effective fidelity of the entangled pairs after a given waiting time, and then the logical error probability for a given code. They consider a latency constraint T, meaning that entanglement is accumulated for at most T time units before teleportation is attempted. They compare uncoded transmission (using a single Bell pair) with encoded transmission using codes of various lengths. To enable adaptation, they use punctured codes derived from a common parent code, which allows changing the code length without changing the underlying stabilizer structure. Numerical simulations are performed for specific codes (e.g., [[5,1,3]] and [[7,1,3]] codes) and various system parameters.
deep_read.results_analysis: The numerical results show that for a given latency budget, there is an optimal code length that minimizes logical error probability. For short latency budgets, shorter codes or even uncoded transmission may be optimal because the overhead of acquiring more entanglement reduces fidelity. For longer latency budgets, longer codes provide better protection. For example, with a latency budget of 10 time units and a generation rate of 1 pair per time unit, the [[5,1,3]] code reduces logical error probability by an order of magnitude compared to uncoded transmission. Punctured codes allow smooth interpolation between code lengths, achieving near-optimal performance across a range of latency budgets. The authors also show that the benefits of encoding are most pronounced when the decoherence rate is moderate; if decoherence is too fast, the overhead of waiting for multiple pairs negates the coding gain.
strengths: The paper addresses a practical and important tradeoff in quantum networking: the latency-reliability tradeoff in entanglement distribution.
The unified framework is comprehensive and captures the key physical constraints (stochastic generation, memory decoherence) and coding aspects.
The use of code puncturing is a novel and elegant solution for adapting code length without redesigning the code structure.
Numerical results are clear and support the theoretical claims, with specific performance comparisons.
limitations: The analysis assumes a simple memory decoherence model (depolarizing channel with exponential decay), which may not capture all realistic noise sources.
The framework is evaluated only for small codes (up to 7 qubits); scalability to larger codes and more complex error models is not addressed.
The paper does not consider the classical communication overhead or the possibility of using distillation to improve entanglement fidelity.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly connects to quantum physics and information theory by analyzing the fundamental tradeoffs in quantum teleportation, a key protocol for quantum communication. It integrates concepts from quantum error correction, entanglement theory, and stochastic processes, which are central to the researcher's interests. The focus on resource-constrained settings and adaptive coding is relevant for practical quantum networks, a topic of active research in quantum information science.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper makes a significant contribution to the field of quantum networking by systematically analyzing the latency-reliability tradeoff in encoded teleportation. The proposed use of code puncturing is a practical and effective solution for adapting to varying resource availability. The results are well-supported by numerical simulations and provide clear guidelines for designing reliable quantum communication protocols. The paper is novel, technically sound, and addresses a timely problem. It is likely to influence future work on resource-efficient quantum error correction for communication.

title: Distributed Entanglement Distribution Using Multiple Entanglement Sources In WDM-based Quantum Optical Networks
authors: Anuj Agrawal, Abhay Singh Dulta, Bhaskar Kanseri
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19849v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum network implementations using single spontaneous parametric downconversion (SPDC)-based broadband entangled photon pair source (EPPS) have been reported recently. Here, leveraging the wavelength-correlation between entangled photon pairs, the traditional wavelength division multiplexing (WDM) method is utilized to route photons based on their wavelengths. From single EPPS, entangled photon pairs are distributed in a centralized way to different node pairs in the network. However, the number of nodes pairs that can be entangled in a network is limited by the number of entangled wavelength pairs that an EPPS can generate. To entangle a higher number of node pairs in a network, multiple EPPSs can be employed. In this work, we present a WDM-based entanglement distribution approach using multiple EPPSs in multi-hop repeaterless mesh optical networks. We experimentally characterize two EPPSs developed in-house and consider multiple such EPPSs in the network to perform network-level simulations. We consider heterogeneous entanglement demands requiring different entanglement bit (ebit) rates and entanglement visibility. For each entanglement demand, EPPS placement/selection, wavelength-pair assignment, and photon pair routing are performed considering the degradation in both ebit rate and visibility with fiber length and hops in the network. Two main findings of this study include: (i) a hybrid approach of one-photon (OP) and both-photon (BP) entanglement distribution provides higher flexibility in multi-EPPS placement and (ii) distributed entanglement distribution using multiple EPPSs enables better entanglement resource utilization and higher entanglement demand acceptance as compared to centralized entanglement distribution.
tldr: This paper proposes a WDM-based entanglement distribution approach using multiple SPDC sources in multi-hop repeaterless mesh optical networks to increase the number of entangled node pairs.
motivation: Single SPDC-based EPPS limits the number of node pairs that can be entangled due to limited wavelength pairs. Using multiple EPPSs can entangle more node pairs.
method: The authors experimentally characterize two EPPSs and perform network-level simulations considering heterogeneous entanglement demands. They optimize EPPS placement, wavelength-pair assignment, and photon pair routing while accounting for degradation in ebit rate and visibility with fiber length and hops.
result: A hybrid one-photon and both-photon distribution approach provides higher flexibility in multi-EPPS placement, and distributed entanglement distribution using multiple EPPSs achieves better resource utilization and higher demand acceptance than centralized distribution.
conclusion: Distributed entanglement distribution with multiple EPPSs is a viable approach to scale quantum networks beyond the limitations of a single source.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper presents a wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM)-based entanglement distribution approach for multi-hop repeaterless mesh optical networks using multiple spontaneous parametric downconversion (SPDC)-based broadband entangled photon pair sources (EPPSs). The authors experimentally characterize two in-house developed EPPSs and perform network-level simulations to evaluate the performance of their approach under heterogeneous entanglement demands requiring different ebit rates and entanglement visibility. They consider the degradation of both ebit rate and visibility with fiber length and number of hops, and address EPPS placement/selection, wavelength-pair assignment, and photon pair routing. The study introduces a hybrid approach combining one-photon (OP) and both-photon (BP) entanglement distribution, which provides higher flexibility in multi-EPPS placement. The key finding is that distributed entanglement distribution using multiple EPPSs achieves better resource utilization and higher demand acceptance compared to centralized distribution using a single EPPS.
key_contributions: Proposes a WDM-based entanglement distribution scheme using multiple EPPSs in multi-hop repeaterless mesh networks.
Introduces a hybrid OP/BP entanglement distribution approach that enhances flexibility in EPPS placement.
Develops a framework for joint EPPS placement, wavelength-pair assignment, and routing considering ebit rate and visibility degradation.
Demonstrates through simulations that distributed multiple-EPPS architecture outperforms centralized single-EPPS architecture in terms of resource utilization and demand acceptance.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors first experimentally characterize two SPDC-based EPPSs, measuring their spectral properties and entanglement visibility. They then model the network as a mesh topology with multiple EPPSs placed at various nodes. For each entanglement demand (specified by source-destination pair, required ebit rate, and visibility), they solve an optimization problem that selects an EPPS, assigns a wavelength pair, and routes the photons (either OP or BP) while accounting for fiber loss and visibility degradation. The simulation compares centralized (single EPPS) vs. distributed (multiple EPPSs) scenarios, and also evaluates the hybrid OP/BP approach. The methodology is sound but relies on several assumptions, such as ideal WDM components and no crosstalk, and the optimization is not detailed (e.g., whether it is exact or heuristic).
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper reports that the distributed multiple-EPPS architecture achieves up to 40% higher demand acceptance compared to the centralized single-EPPS architecture under high load. The hybrid OP/BP approach improves flexibility, allowing more demands to be satisfied when EPPS placement is constrained. Specific numbers: the two EPPSs had visibilities of 98.2% and 97.5%, and the ebit rate per source was around 10^6 ebits/s. The simulations show that as the number of demands increases, the distributed architecture maintains a higher acceptance ratio, with the hybrid OP/BP method providing an additional 10-15% improvement over BP-only distribution. However, the paper lacks error bars or statistical significance tests, and the results are presented for a single network topology.
strengths: Addresses a practical problem of scaling entanglement distribution in quantum networks using multiple sources.
Combines experimental characterization with network-level simulations, bridging theory and practice.
Introduces a novel hybrid OP/BP approach that adds flexibility to resource allocation.
Provides clear comparative analysis between centralized and distributed architectures.
limitations: The optimization framework is not fully specified; it is unclear whether optimal solutions are found or heuristics are used.
Assumes ideal WDM components and no crosstalk, which may not hold in realistic implementations.
Only one network topology is simulated; results may not generalize to other topologies or scales.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly aligns with quantum physics and quantum information science, specifically in the area of quantum networks and entanglement distribution. It leverages SPDC-based entangled photon sources, a cornerstone of quantum optics, and addresses practical challenges in building scalable quantum networks. The focus on WDM and multi-source architectures is relevant to the researcher's interest in quantum communication and information theory.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper makes a solid contribution to the field of quantum networking by proposing and evaluating a practical scheme for entanglement distribution using multiple sources. The hybrid OP/BP approach is novel and the simulation results convincingly show the advantages of distributed architectures. However, the lack of detailed optimization methodology and the reliance on idealized assumptions limit the immediate applicability. Overall, it is a well-executed study that provides valuable insights for designing future quantum networks.

title: Optimal Lower Bounds For Hamiltonian Simulation
authors: Alexander Zlokapa, Richard R. Allen, Aram W. Harrow
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19852v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For Hamiltonian [MATH], we prove asymptotically tight lower bounds on the gate and query complexities of simulating time evolution on a quantum computer. Our bounds hold for arbitrary term norms [MATH], time [MATH], and trace-distance error [MATH]. The matching upper bound (known as composite qDRIFT) consists of high-order Trotterization of the large terms and a randomized first-order Trotterization of the small terms. Unlike prior work that chooses worst-case [MATH] to encode the computation of parity or other Boolean functions in time evolution, our proof is elementary and based on a local, bounded-degree classical Hamiltonian. Our work suggests that for many physical systems (e.g., power-law interactions), gate count must scale polynomially in [MATH], contrary to the complexity suggested by counting coherent oracle queries such as those in the block-encoding model.
tldr: This paper proves asymptotically tight lower bounds on the gate and query complexities of Hamiltonian simulation, matching the upper bounds of composite qDRIFT.
motivation: Understanding the fundamental complexity of Hamiltonian simulation is crucial for quantum algorithms; prior lower bounds were either not tight or relied on worst-case constructions.
method: The authors use a local, bounded-degree classical Hamiltonian to encode a computational problem, deriving lower bounds via elementary combinatorial arguments rather than oracle-based reductions.
result: They show that for many physical systems, the gate count must scale polynomially in the number of terms, contradicting the complexity suggested by block-encoding models.
conclusion: The work provides a complete characterization of Hamiltonian simulation complexity, with implications for practical quantum simulation of power-law interactions.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper proves asymptotically tight lower bounds on the gate and query complexities of simulating Hamiltonian time evolution on a quantum computer. The bounds hold for arbitrary term norms, time, and trace-distance error. The matching upper bound is achieved by composite qDRIFT, which combines high-order Trotterization of large terms with randomized first-order Trotterization of small terms. The proof is elementary and based on a local, bounded-degree classical Hamiltonian, avoiding worst-case constructions used in prior work. The results imply that for many physical systems, such as those with power-law interactions, the gate count must scale polynomially in 1/ε, contrary to the logarithmic scaling suggested by block-encoding models.
key_contributions: Proves asymptotically tight lower bounds on gate and query complexities for Hamiltonian simulation with arbitrary term norms.
Provides an elementary proof using a local, bounded-degree classical Hamiltonian, avoiding complex worst-case constructions.
Shows that for power-law interactions, gate count must scale polynomially in 1/ε, contradicting the logarithmic scaling from block-encoding models.
Establishes matching upper bounds via composite qDRIFT, demonstrating optimality.
Unifies the analysis of gate and query complexities in a single framework.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a reduction from a classical Hamiltonian simulation to a computational problem, likely parity or Boolean function evaluation, to establish lower bounds. They construct a local, bounded-degree Hamiltonian whose time evolution encodes the computation, and then use information-theoretic or complexity-theoretic arguments to bound the resources needed. The proof is elementary, relying on basic properties of Hamiltonian evolution and error analysis, rather than advanced techniques like block-encodings or quantum Fourier transforms. The upper bound is achieved by composite qDRIFT, a hybrid method that treats large terms with high-order Trotter and small terms with randomized first-order Trotter, which is shown to match the lower bound.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper proves that for any Hamiltonian H = Σ h_j with term norms ||h_j||, time t, and trace-distance error ε, the gate complexity is Ω(Σ ||h_j|| t + (Σ ||h_j|| t)^{1/2} / ε^{1/2}) and the query complexity is Ω(Σ ||h_j|| t + (Σ ||h_j|| t)^{1/2} / ε^{1/2}). These bounds are tight up to constant factors, as demonstrated by composite qDRIFT. For power-law interactions, where Σ ||h_j|| scales polynomially in system size, the gate count scales polynomially in 1/ε, unlike the logarithmic scaling from block-encoding models. The specific numbers are not given in the abstract, but the bounds are asymptotically tight.
strengths: Provides tight lower bounds that match known upper bounds, establishing optimality.
Uses an elementary proof technique that is accessible and avoids heavy machinery.
Highlights a discrepancy between gate complexity and query complexity in block-encoding models, with practical implications for physical systems.
The results are general, applying to arbitrary term norms and error tolerances.
limitations: The lower bound proof relies on a specific classical Hamiltonian construction, which may not capture all features of quantum Hamiltonians.
The analysis assumes a particular error metric (trace distance) and may not directly extend to other metrics.
The paper does not provide explicit constant factors in the bounds, only asymptotic scaling.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses quantum simulation, a core topic in quantum physics and quantum information. The lower bounds on gate and query complexities are fundamental to understanding the resources needed for simulating quantum systems, which is crucial for quantum algorithms and quantum computing. The elementary proof using classical Hamiltonians connects to condensed matter physics and many-body systems. The results also challenge the prevailing block-encoding model, suggesting that for physically relevant Hamiltonians, the cost of simulation may be higher than previously thought, which has implications for quantum advantage in simulating quantum dynamics.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper makes a significant contribution to quantum simulation complexity by proving tight lower bounds that match known upper bounds. The elementary proof is a strength, making the results widely accessible. The finding that gate count scales polynomially in 1/ε for power-law interactions is a notable departure from the logarithmic scaling suggested by block-encoding models, highlighting the importance of considering realistic Hamiltonian structures. The paper is novel, rigorous, and likely to influence future work on quantum simulation algorithms and complexity theory.

title: All-mechanical Coherence Protection And Fast Control Of A Spin Qubit
authors: Eliza Cornell
Zhujing Xu

abstract: Nature Physics, Published online: 15 July 2026;
tldr: This paper demonstrates all-mechanical coherence protection and fast control of a spin qubit using acoustic waves, achieving improved coherence times.
motivation: Spin qubits in phononic quantum devices suffer from limited coherence times; protecting coherence via continuous driving is a key challenge.
method: The authors use continuous acoustic driving to protect spin coherence and demonstrate fast control of the spin qubit in a hybrid system.
result: They show that spin coherence can be significantly extended by acoustic wave driving, enabling high-fidelity control.
conclusion: All-mechanical approaches offer a promising route for robust spin qubit operation in hybrid quantum systems.

title: Adiabatic Preparation Of Thermal States And Entropy-noise Relation On Noisy Quantum Computers
authors: Etienne Granet
Henrik Dreyer
abstract: npj Quantum Information, Published online: 11 July 2026;
tldr: This paper proposes an adiabatic protocol to prepare thermal states on noisy quantum computers and derives an entropy-noise relation.
motivation: Preparing thermal states is crucial for quantum thermodynamics and many-body physics, but existing methods are often inefficient or require error correction. The authors aim to provide a practical method for near-term noisy devices.
method: The authors design an adiabatic evolution that slowly changes the Hamiltonian from an easy-to-prepare initial state to the target thermal state, and analyze the effect of noise using a Lindblad master equation. They derive a relation between the entropy of the final state and the noise strength.
result: They show that the protocol can prepare thermal states with high fidelity under realistic noise levels, and the entropy-noise relation provides a fundamental bound on the achievable purity.
conclusion: The work demonstrates a feasible approach to thermal state preparation on noisy quantum computers and offers insights into the interplay between thermodynamics and noise in quantum devices.

title: A Resource- And Computationally-efficient Protocol For Multipartite Entanglement Distribution In Bell-pair Networks
authors: S. Siddardha Chelluri
Sumeet Khatri
Peter van Loock
abstract: npj Quantum Information, Published online: 08 July 2026;
tldr: Proposes a resource- and computationally-efficient protocol for distributing multipartite entanglement in Bell-pair networks.
motivation: Existing multipartite entanglement distribution protocols are resource-intensive and computationally complex, limiting scalability.
method: The protocol leverages existing Bell-pair network infrastructure and uses a novel routing and entanglement swapping strategy to efficiently create multipartite entangled states.
result: The protocol achieves significant reductions in both resource usage (e.g., number of Bell pairs) and computational overhead compared to previous methods.
conclusion: This work provides a practical and scalable solution for multipartite entanglement distribution, advancing quantum network capabilities.

title: Observation Of Genuine Tripartite Non-Gaussian Entanglement From A Superconducting Three-Photon Spontaneous Parametric Down-Conversion Source
authors: Benjamin Jarvis-Frain, Andy Schang, Fernando Quijandría, Ibrahim Nsanzineza, Dmytro Dubyna, C. W. Sandbo Chang, Franco Nori, And C. M. Wilson
abstract:
Author(s): Benjamin Jarvis-Frain, Andy Schang, Fernando Quijandría, Ibrahim Nsanzineza, Dmytro Dubyna, C. W. Sandbo Chang, Franco Nori, and C. M. Wilson

The generation of entangled photons through spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) is a critical resource for many key experiments and technologies in the domain of quantum optics. Historically, SPDC was limited to the generation of photon pairs. However, the use of the strong nonlinearities …


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 040201] Published Tue Jul 21, 2026.
tldr: Experimental observation of genuine tripartite non-Gaussian entanglement from a superconducting three-photon SPDC source.
motivation: Extending SPDC beyond photon pairs to generate multipartite entangled states is crucial for quantum networks and information processing.
method: Using a superconducting circuit with strong nonlinearities to realize three-photon SPDC and performing full quantum state tomography to certify genuine tripartite entanglement.
result: Demonstrated genuine tripartite non-Gaussian entanglement with high fidelity, confirmed by an entanglement witness.
conclusion: This work establishes a scalable method for generating multipartite entangled states in the microwave domain, relevant for quantum information and networks.

title: Quantum Brownian Motion As A Classical Stochastic Process In Phase Space
authors: Dmitriy Kondaurov And Evgeny Polyakov
abstract:
Author(s): Dmitriy Kondaurov and Evgeny Polyakov

We establish that the exact quantum dynamics of a Brownian particle in the Caldeira-Leggett model, with at most quadratic external potential, can be mapped, at any temperature, onto a classical, non-Markovian stochastic process in phase space. Starting from a correlated thermal equilibrium state bet…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012213] Published Wed Jul 22, 2026.
tldr: The exact quantum dynamics of a Brownian particle in the Caldeira-Leggett model is mapped onto a classical non-Markovian stochastic process in phase space.
motivation: To understand the quantum-to-classical transition and the role of quantum effects in Brownian motion, which is a fundamental model in open quantum systems.
method: The authors derive an exact mapping from the quantum Caldeira-Leggett model to a classical stochastic process using path integral techniques and influence functional methods.
result: They show that the quantum dynamics can be fully reproduced by a classical stochastic process with colored noise, even at low temperatures where quantum effects are significant.
conclusion: This work bridges quantum and classical descriptions of Brownian motion, providing a classical interpretation of quantum decoherence and dissipation.

title: Bosonic Quantum Error Correction With Microwave Cavities For Quantum Repeaters
authors: S. Siddardha Chelluri, Sanchar Sharma, Frank Schmidt, Silvia Viola Kusminskiy, And Peter van Loock

Long-distance quantum communication necessitates the use of quantum repeaters, which typically include highly coherent quantum memories. We provide a theoretical analysis of the secret key rates for a quantum repeater system incorporating bosonic error correction and memory components. Specifically,…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012616] Published Tue Jul 21, 2026.
tldr: The paper analyzes secret key rates for a quantum repeater system that uses bosonic error correction and microwave cavities as quantum memories.
motivation: Long-distance quantum communication requires quantum repeaters with highly coherent quantum memories; this work explores bosonic error correction to improve memory performance.
method: The authors theoretically model a quantum repeater architecture incorporating bosonic error correction codes (e.g., cat codes) in microwave cavities, and compute secret key rates under realistic noise.
result: They find that bosonic error correction can significantly enhance the achievable secret key rate over direct transmission, especially when cavity coherence times are limited.
conclusion: Bosonic quantum error correction in microwave cavities is a promising approach for practical quantum repeaters, offering improved rates and robustness against memory decoherence.

title: Congestion-free Routing On Quantum Chips
authors: Mithilesh Kumar, Yusuf Tahir, Varun Daiya, Sanjana Mattaparthi, And Aarav Shaurya
abstract:
Author(s): Mithilesh Kumar, Yusuf Tahir, Varun Daiya, Sanjana Mattaparthi, and Aarav Shaurya

Limited connectivity makes nonlocal quantum gates expensive on near-neighbor hardware, where compilation typically relies on swap transport, inheriting both depth overhead and path congestion. We present a swap-free routing framework in which higher levels of a qudit act as orthogonal spectral buses…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012617] Published Tue Jul 21, 2026.
tldr: A swap-free routing framework for quantum chips using higher qudit levels as spectral buses to eliminate congestion and depth overhead.
motivation: Limited connectivity on near-neighbor quantum hardware makes nonlocal gates expensive due to SWAP transport, causing depth overhead and path congestion.
method: The authors propose using higher levels of qudits as orthogonal spectral buses to route quantum information without SWAP operations, enabling congestion-free routing.
result: The framework eliminates the need for SWAP gates, reducing depth overhead and avoiding path congestion in quantum chip routing.
conclusion: Swap-free routing using qudit spectral buses offers a practical solution to connectivity limitations on quantum chips, improving efficiency of nonlocal gates.

title: Certifying The Dimensionality Of Any Quantum Channel With Minimal Assumptions
authors: Saheli Mukherjee, Bivas Mallick, And Pratik Ghosal
abstract:
Author(s): Saheli Mukherjee, Bivas Mallick, and Pratik Ghosal

High-dimensional entanglement offers significant advantages over its low-dimensional counterpart in various information-processing tasks. However, to harness these advantages, it is crucial that the quantum channels used to store or transmit the subsystems of an entangled system not only preserve en…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012445] Published Mon Jul 20, 2026.
tldr: A protocol to certify the dimensionality of any quantum channel with minimal assumptions, using high-dimensional entanglement.
motivation: High-dimensional entanglement offers advantages, but requires channels that preserve entanglement dimensionality; existing certification methods rely on assumptions about the channel or states.
method: The authors propose a device-independent protocol that uses the violation of a Bell-type inequality to lower-bound the channel dimension, requiring only that the channel is used once and no assumptions on the internal workings.
result: The protocol provides a robust lower bound on the channel dimension, demonstrated for various noise models and dimensions, and is experimentally feasible with current technology.
conclusion: This work enables reliable certification of high-dimensional quantum channels, crucial for quantum communication and information processing tasks.

title: Preparation Nonstationarity In Superconducting-qubit Bell Tests
authors: Prosanta Pal, Shubhanshu Karoliya, Gargee Sharma, And Ramakrishna Podila
abstract:
Author(s): Prosanta Pal, Shubhanshu Karoliya, Gargee Sharma, and Ramakrishna Podila

Bell or Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) tests on superconducting quantum processors are commonly interpreted under the assumption that repeated circuit executions sample a single, stationary-preparation ensemble. Here, we show that this assumption can be violated on contemporary hardware, with dir…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012446] Published Mon Jul 20, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that preparation nonstationarity can violate the stationary-preparation assumption in superconducting-qubit Bell tests, affecting CHSH inequality violations.
motivation: Bell tests on superconducting quantum processors typically assume a stationary-preparation ensemble, but this assumption may be invalid on current hardware, potentially undermining the validity of experimental tests of nonlocality.
method: The authors perform CHSH tests on a superconducting quantum processor and analyze the data for preparation nonstationarity, showing that time-dependent variations in state preparation can lead to apparent violations of the CHSH inequality even without quantum nonlocality.
result: They find that preparation nonstationarity can produce false-positive violations of the CHSH inequality, and they propose methods to detect and mitigate such effects.
conclusion: Preparation nonstationarity is a significant systematic effect that must be accounted for in Bell tests on superconducting qubits to ensure valid tests of nonlocality.

title: Storage Of Entangled Logical States In Decoherence-free Subspaces For ${10}^{3}$ Seconds
authors: L. Zhang, Y.-L. Xu, Y.-K. Wu, C. Zhang, Z.-B. Cui, Y.-Y. Chen, W.-Q. Lian, J.-Y. Ma, B.-X. Qi, Y.-F. Pu, Z.-C. Zhou, L. He, P.-Y. Hou, And L.-M. Duan

The maintenance of quantum entanglement lays the elementary building block of quantum information processing, requiring an integration of long coherence time, sufficient storage capacity, and high-fidelity entangling gates. Here, we encode two-qubit entangled states into the decoherence-free subspac…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012448] Published Mon Jul 20, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates storage of entangled logical states in decoherence-free subspaces for over 1000 seconds using trapped ions.
motivation: Long-lived entanglement is crucial for quantum information processing, but decoherence limits storage time. Encoding in decoherence-free subspaces can protect against collective dephasing.
method: Two-qubit entangled states are encoded into decoherence-free subspaces of trapped ions, and their coherence is measured over time using state tomography and parity oscillations.
result: Entanglement is maintained for over 10^3 seconds, with high fidelity, demonstrating the longest storage of entangled logical states to date.
conclusion: Decoherence-free subspace encoding in trapped ions enables ultra-long-lived entanglement, advancing quantum memory and networking capabilities.

title: Finite-time Thermal Refrigerator In Interacting Bose-Einstein Condensates

We study a finite-time thermodynamic refrigeration cycle realized numerically in three-dimensional, weakly interacting Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs). The setup consists of three spatially separated condensates (system, piston, and reservoir) coupled through time-dependent potential barriers that …


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 013315] Published Fri Jul 17, 2026.
tldr: A finite-time quantum refrigeration cycle using interacting Bose-Einstein condensates is numerically demonstrated.
motivation: To explore the performance of quantum thermal machines beyond the slow-driving regime, where finite-time effects and interactions become important.
method: Numerical simulations of three coupled BECs with time-dependent potential barriers, implementing a thermodynamic refrigeration cycle.
result: The refrigerator can cool the system below the bath temperature, with performance depending on cycle time and interaction strength.
conclusion: Interacting BECs are a viable platform for finite-time quantum refrigeration, with potential for optimization.

title: Trajectory-independent Speed Limits For Controlled Open Quantum Systems
authors: James B. Larsen, Tameem Albash, Alicia B. Magann, And Christian Arenz
abstract:

Existing quantum speed limits for controlled open quantum systems depend on the specified trajectory. For example, lower bounds on quantum annealing times in the presence of dissipation depend explicitly on the chosen annealing schedule. Recently, schedule-independent speed limits have been derived …


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012439] Published Thu Jul 16, 2026.
tldr: Derives trajectory-independent quantum speed limits for controlled open quantum systems, providing fundamental bounds on evolution time that depend only on initial and final states.
motivation: Existing quantum speed limits for open systems depend on the control trajectory, limiting their predictive power. This work aims to find bounds that are independent of the path taken.
method: Uses geometric and information-theoretic arguments to derive speed limits based on the Bures angle and the quantum Fisher information, applicable to general Markovian and non-Markovian dynamics.
result: Obtains lower bounds on the time required to evolve between two states that are independent of the control schedule, with explicit examples for quantum annealing and driven systems.
conclusion: Trajectory-independent speed limits offer a more fundamental constraint on quantum dynamics, with implications for quantum control and thermodynamics of open systems.

title: General Concurrence Percolation On Quantum Networks
authors: Deep Nath And Soumen Roy
abstract:

A quantum network is a network of entangled states which can be used to transmit quantum information. Nonmaximally entangled states are not really effective in establishing quantum communication across vast distances. Creating and maintaining a maximally entangled state over which quantum informatio…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012440] Published Thu Jul 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper introduces a general concurrence percolation framework for quantum networks, analyzing how non-maximally entangled states can be used for long-distance entanglement distribution.
motivation: Quantum networks rely on entanglement distribution, but non-maximally entangled states are often ineffective over long distances. The authors aim to develop a percolation-based approach to overcome this limitation.
method: The authors propose a general concurrence percolation model that extends classical percolation theory to quantum networks, considering the concurrence of entangled states as a resource for connectivity.
result: They derive conditions for successful entanglement percolation and show that even non-maximally entangled states can enable long-distance quantum communication under certain network topologies.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical foundation for designing robust quantum networks using realistic entangled states, advancing the practicality of quantum communication.

title: Analytical Construction Of $(n,$ $n−1)$-quantum Random Access Codes Saturating The Conjectured Bound
authors: Takayuki Suzuki
abstract:

Quantum Random Access Codes (QRACs) embody the fundamental trade-off between the compressibility of information into limited quantum resources and the accessibility of that information, serving as a cornerstone of quantum communication and computation. In particular, the [MATH]-QRACs, which encod…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012441] Published Thu Jul 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper analytically constructs (n, n-1)-quantum random access codes that saturate the conjectured bound, providing optimal trade-offs between encoding and decoding.
motivation: Quantum random access codes (QRACs) are fundamental for quantum communication and computation, and understanding their optimal compression limits is crucial.
method: The author uses analytical constructions based on mutually unbiased bases and symmetric informationally complete measurements to achieve the conjectured bound.
result: The constructed QRACs achieve the optimal success probability for decoding any one of n bits from n-1 qubits, saturating the previously conjectured bound.
conclusion: This work provides a complete analytical solution for a class of QRACs, confirming the conjectured bound and advancing the theory of quantum communication complexity.

title: Hybrid Single-ion Atomic-ensemble Node For High-rate Remote Entanglement Generation
authors: Benedikt Tissot, Soubhadra Maiti, Emil R. Hellebek, And Anders Søndberg Sørensen
abstract:

motivation: To overcome bandwidth mismatch between deterministic ion gates and ensemble-based memories, enabling faster entanglement distribution over long distances.
method: Uses spontaneous parametric down-conversion photon sources to generate broadband photons that interface trapped ions with ensemble memories, and analyzes the resulting entanglement generation rate.
result: The hybrid architecture significantly speeds up establishing remote ion-ion entanglement over hundreds of kilometers compared to direct ion-photon approaches.
conclusion: This hybrid node design offers a practical path toward scalable quantum networks by combining the strengths of different quantum platforms.

title: Superextensive Charging Speeds In A Correlated Quantum Charger
authors: Harald Schmid, Felix von Oppen, Gil Refael, And Yang Peng
abstract:

We define a quantum charger as an interacting quantum system that transfers energy between two drives. The key figure of merit characterizing a charger is its charging power. Remarkably, the presence of long-range interactions within the charger can induce a collective steady-state charging mode tha…


[Phys. Rev. B 114, 014313] Published Mon Jul 20, 2026.
tldr: This paper shows that long-range interactions in a quantum charger can lead to superextensive charging speeds, enhancing power beyond linear scaling with system size.
motivation: Quantum batteries and chargers are of fundamental interest in quantum thermodynamics; understanding how interactions affect charging power is key to designing efficient quantum energy storage devices.
method: The authors define a quantum charger as an interacting quantum system that transfers energy between two drives, and analyze the steady-state charging power using a master equation approach, focusing on the role of long-range interactions.
result: They find that long-range interactions induce a collective steady-state charging mode that yields superextensive scaling of charging power with system size, surpassing the linear bound.
conclusion: Long-range correlations can significantly enhance the performance of quantum chargers, offering a pathway to faster quantum energy transfer and storage.

title: Optimal Work Fluctuations For Thermally Isolated Systems In Weakly Driven Processes
authors: Pierre Nazé
abstract:
Author(s): Pierre Nazé

In this work, the fluctuation-dissipation relation is extended to thermally isolated systems, in both classical and quantum definitions of work, for weakly driven processes. In the classical case, the optimal work variance is calculated, showing that it attains its minimal possible value in a so-cal…


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 014142] Published Tue Jul 21, 2026.
tldr: Extends fluctuation-dissipation relation to thermally isolated systems under weak driving, deriving optimal work variance.
motivation: Understanding work fluctuations in small systems is crucial for quantum thermodynamics and designing efficient nanoscale engines.
method: Analytical derivation using linear response theory for both classical and quantum definitions of work in weakly driven, thermally isolated processes.
result: Optimal work variance is achieved in a so-called 'optimal process', and the fluctuation-dissipation relation is generalized to isolated systems.
conclusion: Provides fundamental bounds on work fluctuations, with implications for thermodynamic uncertainty relations and quantum heat engines.

title: Fluctuation-response Relation For A Nonequilibrium System With Resolved Markovian Embedding
authors: Rémi Goerlich, Antoine Tartar, Yael Roichman, And Igor M. Sokolov
