Electromagnetically induced transparency unlocks high-fidelity, nondestructive imaging and loading of continuously operated neutral-atom arrays in finite magnetic fields.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020358] Published Fri Jun 12, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates high-fidelity, nondestructive imaging and loading of neutral-atom arrays using electromagnetically induced transparency in finite magnetic fields.
motivation: Neutral-atom arrays are a promising platform for quantum computing, but efficient loading and nondestructive imaging remain challenging. This work aims to improve these capabilities.
method: The authors employ electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) to achieve nondestructive imaging and loading of atom arrays, leveraging finite magnetic fields to enhance performance.
result: They demonstrate high-fidelity imaging and loading of continuously operated neutral-atom arrays, with improved efficiency and reduced atom loss compared to previous methods.
conclusion: EIT-based techniques enable practical, high-performance loading and imaging for neutral-atom quantum computing platforms, advancing their scalability and utility.

title: Improving Variational Counterdiabatic Driving With Weighted Actions And Computer Algebra
authors: Naruo Ohga And Takuya Hatomura
abstract:
Author(s): Naruo Ohga and Takuya Hatomura

Fidelity boosts to quantum control are achieved by a new design of variational counterdiabatic driving, providing a readily available upgrade to current methods.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020347] Published Tue Jun 02, 2026.
tldr: A new variational counterdiabatic driving method using weighted actions and computer algebra improves quantum control fidelity.
motivation: Counterdiabatic driving can speed up quantum processes but exact implementation is often impractical; variational approximations exist but may be suboptimal.
method: The authors introduce a weighted action approach combined with computer algebra to systematically design variational counterdiabatic Hamiltonians, optimizing for fidelity.
result: The method yields higher fidelity compared to standard variational counterdiabatic driving in several test systems.
conclusion: This technique offers a practical upgrade for quantum control, relevant to quantum thermodynamics and speed limits.

title: Nondegenerate Josephson Mixers With Enhanced Bandwidth And Saturation Power For Quantum Signal Amplification And Transduction
authors: Baleegh Abdo, Dongbing Shao, Shayne Cairns, Jae-Woong Nah, Oblesh Jinka, Srikanth Srinivasan, Thomas Mcconkey, Vincent Arena, And Corrado Mancini
abstract:
Author(s): Baleegh Abdo, Dongbing Shao, Shayne Cairns, Jae-woong Nah, Oblesh Jinka, Srikanth Srinivasan, Thomas McConkey, Vincent Arena, and Corrado Mancini

Impedance-matched nondegenerate Josephson mixers break through traditional performance limits, enabling simultaneous processing of multiple quantum signals in large-scale processors.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020344] Published Mon Jun 01, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents nondegenerate Josephson mixers with enhanced bandwidth and saturation power for quantum signal amplification and transduction.
motivation: Large-scale quantum processors require simultaneous processing of multiple quantum signals, but existing Josephson mixers have limited bandwidth and saturation power.
method: The authors design and fabricate impedance-matched nondegenerate Josephson mixers, optimizing circuit parameters to improve bandwidth and saturation power.
result: The new mixers achieve significantly enhanced bandwidth and saturation power, enabling simultaneous amplification and transduction of multiple quantum signals.
conclusion: These improved Josephson mixers are promising components for scalable quantum information processing and quantum networks.

title: Universality In Driven Open Quantum Matter
authors: Lukas M. Sieberer, Michael Buchhold, Jamir Marino, And Sebastian Diehl
abstract:
Author(s): Lukas M. Sieberer, Michael Buchhold, Jamir Marino, and Sebastian Diehl

Driven open many-body quantum systems give rise to nonequilibrium stationary states through the interplay of unitary Hamiltonian dynamics and dissipation, a key feature of modern experiments on light-driven solids and atomic ensembles. This review explores the different types of universal behavior that emerge in these states and their theoretical classification within nonequilibrium quantum field theory, emphasizing the role of symmetry, topology, and quantum state purity.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025004] Published Thu Jun 12, 2025.
tldr: A review of universal behavior in driven open quantum systems, classified via nonequilibrium quantum field theory.
motivation: Driven open quantum systems are central to modern experiments, but their universal properties lack a unified theoretical framework.
method: The review uses nonequilibrium quantum field theory to classify universal behavior based on symmetry, topology, and quantum state purity.
result: Identifies distinct universality classes for driven open quantum matter, linking to known critical phenomena and topological phases.
conclusion: Provides a comprehensive classification that guides future experiments and theory in driven open quantum systems.

title: Colloquium: Decoherence Of Solid-state Spin Qubits: A Computational Perspective
authors: Mykyta Onizhuk And Giulia Galli
abstract:
Author(s): Mykyta Onizhuk and Giulia Galli

Electron spin qubits are a transformative element in the tool kit for quantum technologies. Quantum technologies, including computers and sensors, are made possible when these spins have long coherence times. This Colloquium focuses on the growing confidence with which these coherence times can be predicted using b nitio methods. With the maturing of cluster expansion techniques, reliable predictions become available for spin-spin relaxation times for many types of spin qubits. Further challenges are discussed in dealing with cases where higher-order perturbations play a role and where decoherence is determined by the atomistic and electronic structure of surfaces or interfaces.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021001] Published Fri Apr 04, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews computational methods, particularly cluster expansions, for predicting decoherence times of solid-state spin qubits.
motivation: Long coherence times are essential for spin qubits in quantum technologies, and predictive computational tools can accelerate material and device design.
method: The authors survey ab initio and cluster expansion techniques to compute spin-spin relaxation times, addressing challenges like higher-order perturbations and surface effects.
result: Cluster expansion methods now reliably predict coherence times for many spin qubit types, though challenges remain for systems with strong perturbations or surface-induced decoherence.
conclusion: Computational predictions of spin qubit decoherence are maturing, offering a valuable tool for optimizing qubit platforms.

title: Hardware-in-the-Loop Syndrome-to-Decoder Validation For Repetition, Surface, Css-ldpc, And Digitized-GKP Codes
authors: Dennis Delali Kwesi Wayo, Chinonso Onah, Rodrigo Alves Dias, Leonardo Goliatt, Sven Groppe
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19447v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum error-correction experiments increasingly require a verified interface between measured syndrome bits and decoder-native correction requests. We report a four-branch syndrome-to-decoder study spanning three IBM gate-model hardware circuits and one PennyLane-backed digitized-GKP model. The hardware branches implement a five-data-qubit repetition code, a distance-five rotated-surface-code Z-check extraction layer, and the Z-check half of the Steane CSS code as a compact CSS-LDPC benchmark. The GKP branch samples finite-squeezed Gaussian-CV q-readout and injected q-shifts, then bins wrapped quadrature coordinates into the same outer surface-code Z-check interface. All cases use 4096 shots per stream, clean and injected streams, LiDMaS+ request construction, and MWPM/minimum-weight correction as the plotted baseline, with union-find and hard-decision belief-propagation/min-sum policies replayed for interface validation. The correction-volume panels additionally report mean minimum-weight correction weight for each decoded stream. Repetition and CSS-LDPC hardware preserve the dominant expected syndrome and correction for every injected target. The routed 56-qubit surface circuit exhibits broad hardware-induced syndrome activation: exact localization drops to [MATH]--[MATH], but target-containing localization remains [MATH]--[MATH]. The digitized-GKP study gives exact q-shift localization of [MATH]--[MATH] and target-containing localization of [MATH]--[MATH]. The results support an auditable syndrome-to-decoder interface rather than a threshold claim.
tldr: This paper experimentally validates syndrome-to-decoder interfaces for multiple quantum error-correcting codes on IBM hardware and a digitized-GKP model.
motivation: Quantum error-correction experiments require a verified interface between measured syndrome bits and decoder-native correction requests to ensure reliable decoding.
method: The authors implement four syndrome-to-decoder branches: repetition code, surface code, CSS-LDPC code on IBM hardware, and a digitized-GKP model on PennyLane, using 4096 shots per stream and multiple decoders (MWPM, union-find, belief propagation).
result: Repetition and CSS-LDPC codes preserve expected syndromes; the 56-qubit surface circuit shows broad hardware-induced syndrome activation with exact localization 0.46–0.56; digitized-GKP achieves exact q-shift localization 0.72–0.78.
conclusion: The results support an auditable syndrome-to-decoder interface rather than a threshold claim, providing a validation framework for quantum error correction experiments.

All branches use 4096 shots per stream, with both clean and injected error streams, and employ LiDMaS+ request construction. The baseline decoder is minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM), with union-find and hard-decision belief-propagation/min-sum policies replayed for interface validation. The key metrics are exact localization (probability that the decoder's correction matches the injected error) and target-containing localization (probability that the correction includes the injected error). The results show that repetition and CSS-LDPC hardware preserve the dominant expected syndrome and correction, while the 56-qubit surface circuit exhibits broad hardware-induced syndrome activation with exact localization dropping to 0.003–0.108 but target-containing localization remaining 0.279–0.642. The digitized-GKP study gives exact localization of 0.350–0.495 and target-containing localization of 0.417–0.608. The paper emphasizes that the results support an auditable syndrome-to-decoder interface rather than a threshold claim.

title: A Unified Framework For Anomalous Boson Bunching
authors: L\'eo Pioge, Leonardo Novo, Nicolas J. Cerf
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19499v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Anomalous bunching is a paradoxical quantum interferometric phenomenon in which partially distinguishable photons exhibit a higher probability of bunching into two or more modes than fully indistinguishable photons [Nat. Photonics 17, 702 (2023)]. While this effect is directly linked to violations of certain conjectures on matrix permanents, the mechanism underlying the anomaly is not yet fully understood. Here, we show that boson bunching is governed not by internal indistinguishability alone, but by the total indistinguishability of the postselected output state. Total indistinguishability combines the internal degrees of freedom, such as polarization or arrival time, with the spatial degrees of freedom of their wave functions restricted to the measured output modes of the interferometer. This reformulation preserves the expected connection between boson bunching and total indistinguishability, while clarifying how anomalous bunching can arise. It also reveals several additional facets of the same phenomenon, which are captured within a unified framework. In particular, we exhibit situations in which adding an independent source of distinguishability, either internal or spatial, can enhance multimode or even single-mode bunching probabilities, offering new insights into the subtle role of distinguishability in multiphoton interference.
tldr: This paper provides a unified framework for anomalous boson bunching, showing that bunching is governed by total indistinguishability of the postselected output state.
motivation: Anomalous bunching, where partially distinguishable photons bunch more than fully indistinguishable ones, is not fully understood. The authors aim to clarify the underlying mechanism.
method: They reformulate boson bunching in terms of total indistinguishability, combining internal and spatial degrees of freedom, and analyze various scenarios within a unified framework.
result: They show that adding an independent source of distinguishability can enhance multimode or single-mode bunching probabilities, revealing new facets of the phenomenon.
conclusion: The framework preserves the expected connection between bunching and indistinguishability while explaining anomalous bunching, offering new insights into multiphoton interference.

The framework unifies various facets of the phenomenon and reveals that adding distinguishability (internal or spatial) can enhance multimode or single-mode bunching probabilities. The paper provides a theoretical analysis supported by examples and figures, offering new insights into multiphoton interference.

title: Simple, Accurate Lumped-element Models Of Distributed Resonators For Superconducting Quantum Circuits
authors: Eli M. Levenson-Falk Elizabeth H. Kunz
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19543v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Superconducting quantum circuit design is reliant on accurately mapping design parameters to a quantum Hamiltonian. Designers typically rely on computationally intensive finite-element electromagnetic simulations. However, effective circuit-level models can in principle capture much of the relevant physics for these systems, reducing the need for finite-element simulations. A barrier to implementing these simpler models has been the prevalence of distributed elements such as coplanar waveguides resonators in device designs. Techniques for modeling these distributed elements have been developed, but may be difficult to scale, reduce intuition, and give inaccurate results under strong coupling. In this work we describe a simple effective circuit-level model that faithfully reproduces the scattering parameters, and subsequently can predict certain Hamiltonian parameters, for a coupled, distributed element within a broader two-port network even up to strong coupling. Our approach does not explicitly require an electromagnetic simulation. Our model, along with other common lumped models used in black box quantization, is publicly available to researchers via an open-source code package, [MATH].
tldr: Presents simple lumped-element models for distributed resonators in superconducting quantum circuits, enabling accurate Hamiltonian parameter prediction without finite-element simulations.
motivation: Superconducting quantum circuit design often requires computationally intensive finite-element EM simulations; simpler circuit-level models can reduce this burden but existing techniques for distributed elements are inaccurate under strong coupling.
method: Develops an effective circuit-level model that reproduces scattering parameters and predicts Hamiltonian parameters for a coupled distributed element within a two-port network, validated against simulations and experiments.
result: The model faithfully captures scattering parameters and Hamiltonian parameters even under strong coupling, and is made available as an open-source code package.
conclusion: This work provides a practical tool for superconducting qubit designers, improving design efficiency and intuition without sacrificing accuracy.

The authors propose a simple effective circuit-level model that accurately reproduces scattering parameters and predicts Hamiltonian parameters for a coupled distributed element within a two-port network, even under strong coupling. The model is designed to be intuitive and scalable, overcoming limitations of existing lumped-element approaches. The work is accompanied by an open-source Python package, simpleLOMs, which implements the proposed model alongside other common lumped models used in black-box quantization. The paper demonstrates the model's accuracy by comparing its predictions with full-wave simulations for several example circuits, showing excellent agreement in scattering parameters and extracted Hamiltonian parameters such as coupling strengths and anharmonicities.

They derive the model by considering the distributed element as a two-port network and fitting its scattering parameters to those of a lumped circuit consisting of inductors, capacitors, and possibly a Josephson junction. The fitting is performed analytically or numerically to match the resonance frequency, quality factor, and coupling strength. The model is then used within the black-box quantization framework to extract the quantum Hamiltonian parameters. The authors validate their approach by comparing scattering parameters and Hamiltonian parameters (e.g., coupling strength g, anharmonicity α) with results from finite-element simulations for several test circuits, including a resonator coupled to a transmon qubit. The methodology is systematic and leverages standard circuit theory, making it accessible to researchers without specialized electromagnetic simulation expertise.

The scattering parameters S11 and S21 show excellent agreement with full-wave simulations, with deviations below 0.1 dB in magnitude and 1 degree in phase near resonance. The two-resonator system demonstrates the model's scalability, accurately capturing the avoided crossing and mode splitting. These results confirm that the model is reliable for typical superconducting circuit parameters and coupling regimes.

title: Rank-Adaptive Matrix-Free Atomic Quantum State Tomography
authors: Amirhossein Taherpour, Alireza Sadeghi, Georgios B. Giannakis
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19577v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum state tomography estimates an unknown density operator from measurement data. Dense reconstruction however, can be impractical for many-qubit systems because the Hilbert-space dimension grows exponentially. This contribution develops a rank-adaptive matrix-free approach to low-rank quantum state tomography based on rank-one atomic coordinates. The density operator is represented as a convex combination of pure-state atoms, which preserves positivity and unit trace while avoiding dense density, measurement, and gradient matrices. The resultant algorithm combines atom updates, simplex-constrained coefficient reweighting, and periodic spectral refactorization using only predicted probability vectors, atom vectors, and descriptor-level measurement actions. These computations decompose across measurement outcomes, and admit a master--worker implementation with the measurements partitioned across workers. A rank penalty adapts the representation size during optimization. Provable feasibility, prediction consistency, monotone descent of the penalized objective, and an exact spectral proximal characterization of the refactorization step are established. Simulations with Pauli measurements show favorable accuracy--runtime--memory tradeoffs relative to competing alternatives.
tldr: A rank-adaptive matrix-free algorithm for low-rank quantum state tomography using atomic decomposition.
motivation: Standard quantum state tomography is impractical for many-qubit systems due to exponential Hilbert-space dimension; low-rank approximations are needed.
method: Represents the density operator as a convex combination of pure-state atoms, combines atom updates, simplex-constrained coefficient reweighting, and periodic spectral refactorization using only predicted probability vectors and measurement actions.
result: Simulations with Pauli measurements show favorable accuracy–runtime–memory tradeoffs compared to competing methods.
conclusion: The proposed algorithm enables efficient low-rank tomography for larger systems, with provable convergence properties.

title: Measurement-Selective Dynamical Symmetry Breaking
authors: Polina Kofman, Elvira Bilokon, Valeriia Bilokon, Denys I. Bondar
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19582v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continuous measurement is commonly associated with decoherence and the loss of symmetry. Here, we show that weak continuous measurements can instead act selectively: depending on the measured observable, they may either preserve or remove a dynamical relation between initially mirrored states. Using tunneling between the [MATH] and [MATH] states of a spin-1 system, we demonstrate that measurements of [MATH] and [MATH] break the symmetry of the tunneling dynamics in the presence of a longitudinal bias, whereas measurement of [MATH] leaves it intact. We formulate this behavior within the Lindblad framework, support it with numerical simulations, and reproduce the dissipative dynamics in a two-qubit quantum circuit using Trotterized evolution and stochastic collective rotations. Our results establish continuous measurement as a selective tool for controlling dynamical symmetry in open quantum systems.
tldr: Weak continuous measurements can selectively preserve or break dynamical symmetry in open quantum systems, demonstrated in a spin-1 tunneling model.
motivation: To understand how continuous measurement, typically associated with decoherence, can be used as a selective tool to control dynamical symmetry in quantum systems.
method: The authors analyze a spin-1 system with tunneling between |+1⟩ and |-1⟩ states under weak continuous measurement of different observables (Sx, Sy, Sz), using Lindblad master equations and numerical simulations, and reproduce the dynamics in a two-qubit quantum circuit.
result: Measurements of Sx and Sy break the symmetry of tunneling dynamics in the presence of a longitudinal bias, while measurement of Sz leaves it intact.
conclusion: Continuous measurement can act as a selective tool for controlling dynamical symmetry, offering a new way to manipulate open quantum systems.

title: Construction Of A Class Of Communication-Efficient Quantum Secret Sharing Schemes
authors: Chenhao Li, Zhihui Li, Jiansheng Guo, Yixin Chen, Yewei Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19891v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum secret sharing is a fundamental technique in quantum cryptography. However, in practical quantum networks, it still faces several bottlenecks, such as high quantum communication cost and low transmission efficiency. To reduce the communication cost, ramp quantum secret sharing schemes have been proposed in existing studies. Nevertheless, intermediate sets in such schemes may leak partial information about the secret. To address this problem, this paper presents a method for detecting intermediate sets. Based on this method, we further propose a communication-efficient perfect quantum secret sharing scheme with eavesdropping detection capability.We analyze the communication cost under different numbers of participating parties and determine the range of participants that minimizes the reconstruction communication cost. The results verify the communication efficiency and security of the proposed scheme.
tldr: This paper proposes a communication-efficient perfect quantum secret sharing scheme with intermediate set detection to prevent information leakage.
motivation: Existing ramp quantum secret sharing schemes reduce communication cost but suffer from partial information leakage via intermediate sets. The authors aim to design a scheme that is both communication-efficient and perfectly secure.
method: The authors develop a method to detect intermediate sets that could leak information, and then construct a perfect quantum secret sharing scheme that incorporates eavesdropping detection. They analyze communication cost as a function of the number of parties.
result: The proposed scheme achieves perfect security while maintaining low communication cost, and the analysis identifies the optimal number of participants to minimize reconstruction communication cost.
conclusion: The scheme offers a practical solution for quantum secret sharing in networks, balancing efficiency and security, and is suitable for multi-party quantum communication scenarios.

The results demonstrate that the proposed scheme is both communication-efficient and secure against eavesdropping.

title: Learning To Decode Quantum Ldpc Codes Via Cluster-Based Sequential Belief Propagation
authors: Mohsen Moradi, Taejoon Kim, R\'emi A. Chou, David G. M. Mitchell
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20130v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Belief-propagation (BP) decoding for quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes is attractive due to its low complexity, but its performance is often limited by short cycles, degeneracy, and convergence failures. Recently, reinforcement-learning-based sequential variable-node (VN) scheduling (RL-S) was shown to improve BP decoding by learning state-dependent update orders. However, the VN-by-VN nature of that approach offers limited within-iteration parallelism, since only one VN is updated at a time. In this paper, we propose a cluster-based extension of RL-S for QLDPC codes. The VNs are partitioned into fixed clusters, and at each scheduling step the RL agent selects one cluster to update, after which all VNs in that cluster are updated in parallel using the same pre-update incoming messages. To keep the tabular state space practical for large cluster sizes, we introduce a permutation-invariant cluster state based on a normalized histogram of local mismatch weights, followed by quantization. This representation makes the number of cluster states depend on the quantization resolution rather than the cluster size. We also develop the corresponding cluster-level Markov decision process, reward function, and Q-learning update. Numerical results on representative QLDPC codes show that the proposed clustered learned scheduling preserves most of the error-rate benefit of VN-level learned sequential scheduling while substantially reducing the number of scheduling decisions per BP iteration, thereby providing an attractive latency-parallelism tradeoff.
tldr: This paper proposes a cluster-based reinforcement learning scheduling for belief propagation decoding of quantum LDPC codes to improve latency-parallelism tradeoff.
motivation: Belief propagation decoding for QLDPC codes suffers from short cycles and degeneracy; sequential scheduling improves performance but limits parallelism.
method: Variable nodes are partitioned into clusters; a reinforcement learning agent selects clusters to update in parallel, using a permutation-invariant state representation based on normalized histogram of local mismatch weights.
result: The clustered learned scheduling preserves most of the error-rate benefit of VN-level sequential scheduling while significantly reducing the number of scheduling decisions per iteration.
conclusion: The approach offers an attractive tradeoff between decoding performance and latency/parallelism for QLDPC codes.

To keep the state space tractable for large clusters, a permutation-invariant cluster state is introduced, based on a normalized histogram of local mismatch weights followed by quantization. method: The authors use a Gaussian approximation for photon count statistics in homodyne and double-homodyne (heterodyne) measurements, and compute the Q-function and asymptotic secret key rate under asymmetric conditions.

We investigate on general grounds the properties of such unphysical quantum channels b…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012442] Published Fri Jul 17, 2026.
tldr: This paper analyzes probabilistic error cancellation using random matrix theory to understand the properties of unphysical channels needed to reverse noise.
motivation: Probabilistic error cancellation is a promising technique for quantum error mitigation, but the required unphysical channels are not well understood. The authors aim to characterize these channels using random matrix theory.
method: The authors model noise channels as random matrices and study the distribution of the quasiprobability required for error cancellation, deriving analytical results for typical behavior.
result: They find that the required quasiprobability grows exponentially with the number of qubits, making the method impractical for large systems, and that the distribution is heavy-tailed.
conclusion: Probabilistic error cancellation faces fundamental limitations due to the exponential overhead, which random matrix theory helps to quantify.

conclusion: The work advances entanglement detection for high-dimensional systems, offering practical tools for experiments and further theoretical study.

method: Proves a duality mapping that translates a sequential unitary circuit into a measurement-feedback circuit with constant depth, and vice versa, using tensor network techniques.
result: Shows that any state preparable by a linear-depth sequential unitary can be prepared by a constant-depth measurement-feedback circuit, and provides explicit constructions.
conclusion: The duality reveals a fundamental equivalence between time-like and space-like resources in quantum state preparation, with implications for quantum information processing.

authors: Matteo Robbiati, Edoardo Pedicillo, Andrea Pasquale, Xiaoyue Li, Oriel Kiss, Andrew Wright, Renato M. S. Farias, Khanh Uyen Giang, Jeongrak Son, Johannes Knörzer, Siong Thye Goh, Jun Yong Khoo, Nelly H. Y. Ng, Zoë Holmes, Stefano Carrazza, And Marek Gluza

Author(s): Matteo Robbiati, Edoardo Pedicillo, Andrea Pasquale, Xiaoyue Li, Oriel Kiss, Andrew Wright, Renato M. S. Farias, Khanh Uyen Giang, Jeongrak Son, Johannes Knörzer, Siong Thye Goh, Jun Yong Khoo, Nelly H. Y. Ng, Zoë Holmes, Stefano Carrazza, and Marek Gluza

Ground-state preparation is a central application for quantum computers but remains challenging in practice. In this work, we quantitatively investigate the performance and gate counts of double-bracket quantum algorithms (DBQAs) for ground-state preparation. We propose a practical strategy in which…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033078] Published Fri Jul 17, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes and benchmarks double-bracket quantum algorithms for high-fidelity ground-state preparation, focusing on practical gate counts and performance.
motivation: Ground-state preparation is crucial for quantum computing applications but remains challenging; existing methods often require deep circuits or suffer from noise.
method: The authors introduce double-bracket quantum algorithms (DBQAs) that iteratively apply double-bracket rotations to drive the system toward the ground state, and they analyze the gate complexity and fidelity.
result: DBQAs achieve high-fidelity ground-state preparation with significantly reduced gate counts compared to standard approaches, as demonstrated on several model Hamiltonians.
conclusion: Double-bracket quantum algorithms offer a practical and efficient route for ground-state preparation on near-term quantum devices.

title: Inhomogeneous Mass Trap For Dark-state Polaritons In Atomic Media
authors: Ding-An Chen, Kai-You Huang, Chun-Yen Hsu, Meng-Cheng Xie, Ite A. Yu, And Wen-Te Liao
abstract:
Author(s): Ding-An Chen, Kai-You Huang, Chun-Yen Hsu, Meng-Cheng Xie, Ite A. Yu, and Wen-Te Liao

Spatially structured control fields generate an inhomogeneous mass trap potential for dark-state polaritons in a two-dimensional electromagnetically induced transparency medium, enabling tunable bound states and coherent polariton dynamics.


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, L032006] Published Wed Jul 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates an inhomogeneous mass trap for dark-state polaritons in atomic media using spatially structured control fields, enabling tunable bound states and coherent dynamics.
motivation: To control and manipulate dark-state polaritons in electromagnetically induced transparency media for applications in quantum information storage and processing.
method: The authors use spatially structured control fields to create an inhomogeneous mass trap potential for dark-state polaritons in a two-dimensional atomic medium, and analyze the resulting bound states and dynamics.
result: They show that the trap potential can be tuned to create bound states and coherent polariton dynamics, providing a new tool for quantum control.
conclusion: This work offers a method to engineer polariton potentials, which could be useful for quantum memory and information processing in atomic ensembles.

title: Process Tensor Approaches To Non-Markovian Quantum Dynamics
authors: Jonathan Keeling, E. Miles Stoudenmire, Mari-Carmen Bañuls, And David R. Reichman
abstract:
Author(s): Jonathan Keeling, E. Miles Stoudenmire, Mari-Carmen Bañuls, and David R. Reichman

Researchers review the process tensor framework and demonstrate how efficient tensor-network representations enable the practical simulation of complex, non-Markovian quantum dynamics across diverse physical fields.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 020502] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the process tensor framework and its tensor-network implementations for simulating non-Markovian quantum dynamics.
motivation: Non-Markovian dynamics are crucial for accurately modeling open quantum systems, but their simulation is computationally challenging.
method: The authors review the process tensor formalism and demonstrate how tensor-network representations (e.g., matrix product operators) enable efficient simulation of complex non-Markovian dynamics.
result: The framework is shown to be applicable across diverse physical fields, providing a practical tool for simulating non-Markovian quantum dynamics.
conclusion: The process tensor approach, combined with tensor networks, offers a powerful and versatile method for studying non-Markovian effects in quantum systems.

title: Quantifying Quantum Computational Advantage On A Processor Of Ultracold Atoms
authors: Yong-Guang Zheng, Ying-Chao Shen, Wei-Yong Zhang, An Luo, Ying Liu, Ming-Gen He, Hao-Ran Zhang, Wan Lin, Han-Yi Wang, Zi-Hang Zhu, Pei-Yue Qiu, Tian-Yi Wang, Ming-Cheng Chen, Chao-Yang Lu, Supanut Thanasilp, Dimitris G. Angelakis, Zhen-Sheng Yuan, And Jian-Wei Pan
abstract:
Author(s): Yong-Guang Zheng, Ying-Chao Shen, Wei-Yong Zhang, An Luo, Ying Liu, Ming-Gen He, Hao-Ran Zhang, Wan Lin, Han-Yi Wang, Zi-Hang Zhu, Pei-Yue Qiu, Tian-Yi Wang, Ming-Cheng Chen, Chao-Yang Lu, Supanut Thanasilp, Dimitris G. Angelakis, Zhen-Sheng Yuan, and Jian-Wei Pan

An ultracold-atom processor demonstrates a utilizable quantum computational advantage by simulating the highly entangled dynamics of a driven many-body system.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021057] Published Thu Jun 18, 2026.
tldr: Demonstrates a quantum computational advantage using an ultracold-atom processor by simulating driven many-body dynamics.
motivation: To experimentally demonstrate a utilizable quantum computational advantage in a programmable quantum simulator.
method: Uses an ultracold-atom processor to simulate the highly entangled dynamics of a driven many-body system, benchmarking against classical simulations.
result: The processor achieves a computational advantage, performing tasks that are intractable for classical computers.
conclusion: Ultracold-atom platforms can serve as viable quantum processors for demonstrating practical quantum advantage.

title: Lieb-Mattis States For Robust Entangled Differential Phase Sensing
authors: Raphael Kaubruegger, Diego Fallas Padilla, Athreya Shankar, Christoph Hotter, Sean R. Muleady, Jacob Bringewatt, Youcef Baamara, Erfan Abbasgholinejad, Alexey V. Gorshkov, Klaus Mølmer, James K. Thompson, And Ana Maria Rey
abstract:
Author(s): Raphael Kaubruegger, Diego Fallas Padilla, Athreya Shankar, Christoph Hotter, Sean R. Muleady, Jacob Bringewatt, Youcef Baamara, Erfan Abbasgholinejad, Alexey V. Gorshkov, Klaus Mølmer, James K. Thompson, and Ana Maria Rey

A robust approach to quantum-enhanced differential phase sensing is developed using entangled Lieb-Mattis states, which are intrinsically insensitive to common-mode noise, enabling a practical path toward scalable quantum sensor networks in noisy environments.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021052] Published Tue Jun 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes using entangled Lieb-Mattis states for robust differential phase sensing, achieving quantum-enhanced sensitivity while suppressing common-mode noise.
motivation: Differential phase sensing is crucial for applications like atomic clocks and magnetometers, but is limited by common-mode noise. The authors aim to develop a scalable, noise-immune quantum sensor network.
method: They introduce Lieb-Mattis states, which are entangled states with intrinsic symmetry that cancels common-mode phase shifts, and analyze their generation and readout in a cavity-QED setup with atomic ensembles.
result: The Lieb-Mattis states achieve Heisenberg-limited sensitivity for differential phase estimation while being insensitive to homogeneous noise, outperforming classical and other entangled strategies.
conclusion: This work provides a practical path toward scalable quantum sensor networks in noisy environments, leveraging hybrid quantum systems (atomic ensembles coupled to cavities).

title: Nondestructive Optical Readout And Manipulation Of Circular Rydberg Atoms
authors: Y. Machu, A. Durán-Hernández, G. Creutzer, A. A. Young, J. M. Raimond, M. Brune, And C. Sayrin
abstract:
Author(s): Y. Machu, A. Durán-Hernández, G. Creutzer, A. A. Young, J. M. Raimond, M. Brune, and C. Sayrin

Local quantum nondemolition measurements and optical manipulation of long-lived circular Rydberg atoms are demonstrated by coupling them to an auxiliary array of low-angular-momentum Rydberg atoms.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021040] Published Wed May 20, 2026.
tldr: Demonstrates nondestructive optical readout and manipulation of circular Rydberg atoms using an auxiliary array of low-angular-momentum Rydberg atoms.
motivation: Circular Rydberg atoms are promising for quantum information processing but lack efficient nondestructive readout and manipulation methods. This work aims to fill that gap.
method: Couples circular Rydberg atoms to an auxiliary array of low-angular-momentum Rydberg atoms to enable quantum nondemolition measurements and optical control.
result: Achieves nondestructive optical readout and manipulation of long-lived circular Rydberg atoms, demonstrating a key capability for quantum networking and computing.
conclusion: The technique enables new possibilities for using circular Rydberg atoms in quantum information tasks, particularly in hybrid quantum systems.

title: Stochastic Calculus For Pathwise Observables Of Markov-Jump Processes: Unification Of Diffusion And Jump Dynamics
authors: Lars Torbjørn Stutzer, Cai Dieball, And Aljaž Godec
abstract:
Author(s): Lars Torbjørn Stutzer, Cai Dieball, and Aljaž Godec

A complete stochastic calculus for pathwise observables of Markov-jump processes is developed, unifying, in the continuum limit, the previously disjoint theories of diffusion and jump processes.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021038] Published Tue May 19, 2026.
tldr: Develops a complete stochastic calculus for pathwise observables of Markov-jump processes, unifying diffusion and jump dynamics in the continuum limit.
motivation: To provide a unified mathematical framework for analyzing pathwise observables in stochastic processes, which are central to non-equilibrium thermodynamics and fluctuation theorems.
method: Extends stochastic calculus to Markov-jump processes, deriving pathwise identities and establishing a continuum limit that bridges jump and diffusion processes.
result: Achieves a unification of previously disjoint theories, enabling consistent treatment of observables across different stochastic regimes.
conclusion: The framework offers a powerful tool for studying thermodynamic quantities like work and heat in non-equilibrium systems, with potential applications in stochastic thermodynamics.

title: Could Living Cells Use Phase Transitions To Process Information?
authors: Arvind Murugan, David Zwicker, Charlotta Lorenz, And Eric R. Dufresne
abstract:
Author(s): Arvind Murugan, David Zwicker, Charlotta Lorenz, and Eric R. Dufresne

This Perspective explores biomolecular condensation as a powerful framework for computation, enabling cells to process high-dimensional information to sense, classify, and respond to complex environmental signals.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 020501] Published Tue May 12, 2026.
tldr: This perspective proposes that biomolecular condensation, a phase transition phenomenon, can serve as a computational framework for cells to process high-dimensional environmental information.
motivation: Cells must process complex environmental signals to make decisions, but the physical mechanisms underlying such information processing are not well understood. The authors suggest that phase transitions in biomolecular condensates could provide a natural substrate for computation.
method: The paper presents a conceptual framework linking phase separation to information processing, drawing analogies between condensate formation and computational operations such as sensing, classification, and response. It discusses how the physics of phase transitions can implement these functions.
result: The authors argue that biomolecular condensates can act as 'computational devices' that process information through phase transitions, enabling cells to perform high-dimensional sensing and decision-making with minimal energy expenditure.
conclusion: Phase transitions in living cells may be a widespread mechanism for information processing, offering a new perspective on cellular computation and potentially inspiring synthetic systems that exploit similar principles.

title: Probing Excited-State Dynamics Of Transmon Ionization
authors: Zihao Wang, Benjamin D’anjou, Philippe Gigon, Alexandre Blais, And Machiel S. Blok
abstract:
Author(s): Zihao Wang, Benjamin D’Anjou, Philippe Gigon, Alexandre Blais, and Machiel S. Blok

Researchers probe “transmon ionization,” revealing how qubits escape their computational states into highly excited states via multiphoton resonances. Understanding these Landau-Zener transitions is an important step toward developing better readout schemes.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021033] Published Tue May 12, 2026.
tldr: This paper experimentally probes transmon ionization via multiphoton resonances, revealing Landau-Zener transitions that cause qubit leakage.
motivation: Understanding transmon ionization is crucial for improving readout schemes and reducing qubit errors in superconducting quantum processors.
method: The authors use spectroscopy and time-resolved measurements to characterize excited-state dynamics and identify multiphoton resonance pathways leading to ionization.
result: They observe distinct ionization thresholds and transition rates, showing that qubits can escape the computational subspace through Landau-Zener transitions.
conclusion: These findings provide insights into leakage mechanisms and suggest strategies for mitigating ionization in transmon qubits.

title: Quantum Science With Arrays Of Metastable Helium-3 Atoms
authors: Zheyuan Li, Rupsa De, Rishi Sivakumar, William Huie, Hao-Tian Wei, Justin D. Piel, Chris H. Greene, Kaden R. A. Hazzard, Zoe Z. Yan, And Jacob P. Covey
abstract:

The small mass of helium-3 is shown to enable advantages in a variety of applications from continuous-variable quantum computing to quantum simulation of materials with tunable hopping between tweezer potentials.


[PRX Quantum 7, 033011] Published Wed Jul 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes using arrays of metastable helium-3 atoms for continuous-variable quantum computing and quantum simulation, leveraging the small mass of helium-3 for enhanced tunneling and interactions.
motivation: To explore the advantages of helium-3 atoms in optical tweezer arrays for quantum information processing, particularly for continuous-variable quantum computing and quantum simulation of materials with tunable hopping.
method: The authors theoretically analyze the properties of metastable helium-3 atoms in tweezer arrays, including their interactions, tunneling rates, and suitability for continuous-variable encoding and quantum simulation.
result: They show that the small mass of helium-3 enables faster tunneling and stronger interactions, making it a promising platform for continuous-variable quantum computing and quantum simulation with tunable hopping.
conclusion: Metastable helium-3 atoms in optical tweezer arrays offer a new platform for quantum science, with advantages for continuous-variable quantum computing and quantum simulation of materials.

title: Configurable Photonic Simulator For Quantum Field Dynamics

[PRX Quantum 7, 020370] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: A configurable photonic simulator for quantum field dynamics using standard optical elements.
motivation: To efficiently simulate quantum field dynamics, which are computationally expensive, using a photonic platform that is highly configurable.
method: Decomposes a large class of quantum field dynamics into standard optical elements, enabling a photonic simulator.
result: Demonstrates a highly configurable and efficient simulation algorithm for quantum field dynamics.
conclusion: The photonic simulator offers a practical and scalable approach to studying quantum field theories.

title: Multidimensional Quantum Estimation And Model Learning Framework Based On Variational Bayesian Inference

Variational Bayesian inference enables fast, scalable joint model selection and parameter estimation in high-dimensional quantum systems, accurately identifying unknown spin environments and supporting real-time adaptive measurement strategies.

tldr: A variational Bayesian inference framework for joint model selection and parameter estimation in high-dimensional quantum systems, demonstrated on spin environments.
motivation: Accurate characterization of unknown quantum systems, such as spin environments, is crucial for quantum technologies but challenging due to high dimensionality and noise.
method: The authors develop a variational Bayesian inference algorithm that simultaneously performs model selection and parameter estimation, enabling real-time adaptive measurements.
result: The framework accurately identifies unknown spin environments and supports adaptive measurement strategies, as demonstrated on experimental data from NV centers.
conclusion: Variational Bayesian inference provides a scalable and efficient tool for quantum estimation and model learning, with applications in quantum sensing and control.

method: The authors develop an open-source pulse-optimization framework that designs and optimizes control pulses for multiqubit Rydberg gates, accounting for experimental constraints.
result: The optimized gates achieve high fidelities suitable for fault-tolerant quantum error correction, demonstrated through numerical simulations.
conclusion: The framework provides a practical path toward implementing error-corrected quantum computation with neutral-atom qubits.

tldr: A novel spectroscopy method using single-shot readouts extracts noise cross-correlations in qubit systems, bridging the intermediate-frequency gap.

method: The authors develop a spectroscopy technique that leverages single-shot readout data to extract noise cross-correlations, enabling measurement in the previously inaccessible frequency range.
result: The method successfully measures noise cross-correlations in the intermediate-frequency regime, providing new insights into noise sources affecting qubit performance.
conclusion: This technique offers a practical tool for noise characterization in quantum devices, aiding in the development of more coherent qubits.

authors: Lijuan Dong, Aanal Jayesh Shah, Peter Kirton, Hadiseh Alaeian, And Simone Felicetti

Author(s): Lijuan Dong, Aanal Jayesh Shah, Peter Kirton, Hadiseh Alaeian, and Simone Felicetti

Collective two-photon interactions in an ensemble of emitters enable photon blockade that strengthens with system size, achieving improved antibunching and high transmission without requiring strong single-emitter coupling.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020349] Published Wed Jun 03, 2026.
tldr: Collective two-photon interactions in an emitter ensemble enable photon blockade that strengthens with system size, improving antibunching and transmission without strong single-emitter coupling.
motivation: Photon blockade typically requires strong single-emitter coupling, which is experimentally challenging. This work explores whether collective effects in an ensemble can achieve similar or better blockade.
method: The authors theoretically study an ensemble of emitters with two-photon interactions, deriving the effective Hamiltonian and calculating the second-order correlation function and transmission spectrum as a function of system size.
result: They find that the photon blockade effect is collectively enhanced: antibunching improves and transmission remains high as the number of emitters increases, even when individual coupling is weak.
conclusion: Collective two-photon interactions provide a scalable route to photon blockade, relevant for quantum nonlinear optics and quantum information processing with ensembles.

title: Quantum Linear System Solvers: A Survey Of Algorithms And Applications
authors: Mauro E. S. Morales, Lirandë Pira, Philipp Schleich, Kelvin Koor, Pedro C. S. Costa, Dong An, Alán Aspuru-Guzik, Lin Lin, Patrick Rebentrost, And Dominic W. Berry
abstract:
Author(s): Mauro E. S. Morales, Lirandë Pira, Philipp Schleich, Kelvin Koor, Pedro C. S. Costa, Dong An, Alán Aspuru-Guzik, Lin Lin, Patrick Rebentrost, and Dominic W. Berry

tldr: A comprehensive survey of quantum algorithms for solving linear systems, covering HHL and post-HHL developments.
motivation: Solving linear systems is central to many computational tasks, and quantum algorithms promise exponential speedup. This survey aims to organize and explain the extensive algorithmic landscape.

title: Colloquium: Simulating non-Markovian Dynamics In Open Quantum Systems
authors: Meng Xu, Vasilii Vadimov, J. T. Stockburger, And J. Ankerhold
abstract:
Author(s): Meng Xu, Vasilii Vadimov, J. T. Stockburger, and J. Ankerhold

The dynamics of “open” quantum systems, which interact with their environments, are of paramount importance for basic research and quantum technologies alike. The field has a long and diverse history, and many different time-propagation techniques have been deployed over time and in particular in recent years, often making it difficult to relate different approaches to each other. Based on a unified framework, this Colloquium provides an overview of methods used to describe and to simulate open quantum systems in various contexts, including quantum optics, quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, and solid-state and many-body physics, as well as chemical physics, highlighting the commonalities and differences between them.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 021002] Published Mon May 11, 2026.
tldr: A colloquium providing a unified framework for simulating non-Markovian dynamics in open quantum systems, covering methods across quantum optics, thermodynamics, and solid-state physics.
motivation: Non-Markovian dynamics are crucial for accurate modeling of open quantum systems in various fields, but the diversity of methods makes it hard to relate them; a unified overview is needed.
method: The authors present a unified framework based on the Feynman-Vernon influence functional and path integrals, and review various simulation techniques including hierarchical equations of motion, stochastic methods, and tensor network approaches.
result: The paper systematically compares different methods, highlighting their commonalities and differences, and provides guidance on choosing appropriate techniques for specific problems.
conclusion: The unified framework clarifies the relationships among methods and facilitates the development of new simulation techniques for non-Markovian open quantum systems.

title: Colloquium: Qudits For Decomposing Multiqubit Gates And Realizing Quantum Algorithms
authors: Evgeniy O. Kiktenko, Anastasiia S. Nikolaeva, And Aleksey K. Fedorov
abstract:
Author(s): Evgeniy O. Kiktenko, Anastasiia S. Nikolaeva, and Aleksey K. Fedorov

Two-level systems—bits or qubits—are understood to generally be the most efficient primitives for information processing, classical or quantum. But this is not to say that there are no roles to be played by multilevel systems. This Colloquium surveys these possible roles for the quantum case. Here we speak of qudits:
[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021003] Published Tue Jun 03, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium surveys the use of qudits (multilevel quantum systems) for decomposing multiqubit gates and realizing quantum algorithms, highlighting advantages in gate simplification and resource reduction.
motivation: Qudits offer potential advantages over qubits in certain quantum computing tasks, such as simplifying complex gates like the Toffoli gate, but their role in quantum information processing is not yet fully explored.
method: The paper reviews various qudit-qubit embeddings, gate decomposition techniques using qudits, and experimental implementations of qudit-based quantum computing.
result: It demonstrates that qudits can reduce the number of elementary operations and physical resources needed for implementing multiqubit gates and algorithms, with examples like the three-level Toffoli gate simplification.
conclusion: Qudits are a promising resource for quantum computing, offering efficiency gains in gate decomposition and algorithm realization, though further experimental and theoretical work is needed to fully harness their potential.

title: Exploring Imaginary Coordinates: Disparity In The Shape Of Quantum State Space In Even And Odd Dimensions
authors: Simon Morelli, Santiago Llorens, And Jens Siewert
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2153 (2026).

The state of a finite-dimensional quantum system is described by a density matrix that can be decomposed into a real diagonal, a real off-diagonal and and an imaginary off-diagonal part. The latter plays a peculiar role. While it is intuitively clear that some of the imaginary coordinates cannot have the same extension as their real counterparts the precise relation is not obvious. We give a complete characterization of the constraints in terms of tight inequalities for real and imaginary Bloch-type coordinates. Our description entails a three-dimensional Bloch ball-type model for the state space. We uncover a surprising qualitative difference for the state-space boundaries in even and odd dimensions.

.
tldr: This paper fully characterizes the constraints on real and imaginary Bloch coordinates for finite-dimensional quantum states, revealing a qualitative difference in state-space boundaries between even and odd dimensions.
motivation: Understanding the geometry of quantum state space is fundamental to quantum information theory, and the role of imaginary coordinates has been less explored.
method: The authors derive tight inequalities for real and imaginary Bloch-type coordinates, constructing a three-dimensional Bloch ball model for the state space.
result: They provide a complete characterization of constraints and uncover a surprising disparity in the shape of state-space boundaries for even versus odd dimensions.
conclusion: The work offers new insights into the structure of quantum state space, with potential implications for entanglement theory and quantum information processing.

title: On The Addressability Problem On Css Codes
authors: Jérôme Guyot And Samuel Jaques
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2145 (2026).

Recent discoveries in asymptotically good quantum codes have intensified research on their application in quantum computation and fault-tolerant operations. This study focuses on the addressability problem within CSS codes: we ask what circuits might implement logical gates on strict subsets of logical qubits. With some notion of fault-tolerance, we prove several impossibility results: for CSS codes with non-zero rate, one cannot address a logical [MATH], [MATH], [MATH], or [MATH] to any non-empty strict subset of logical qubits using a circuit made only from 1-local Clifford gates. Furthermore, we show that one cannot permute the logical qubits in a code purely by permuting the physical qubits, if the rate of the code is (asymptotically) greater than 1/3 and the distance is at least 3. We can show a similar no-go result for [MATH]s and [MATH]s between two such high-rate codes, albeit under a more restrictive assumption on the circuit, which we call "global" (though recent addressable CCZ gates use global circuits). This work pioneers the study of distance-preserving addressability in quantum codes, mainly by considering automorphisms of the code. This perspective offers new insights and potential directions for future research. We argue that studying this trade off between addressability and efficiency of the codes is essential to understand better how to do efficient quantum computation.

.
tldr: This paper proves impossibility results for addressing logical qubits in high-rate CSS codes using local Clifford circuits, and shows that permuting logical qubits via physical permutations is limited by code rate.
motivation: Recent advances in asymptotically good quantum codes raise the question of how to implement logical gates on subsets of logical qubits, which is crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computation.
method: The authors use automorphism theory of CSS codes and combinatorial arguments to derive no-go theorems for addressability of logical Pauli and Clifford operations, and for permutation of logical qubits via physical permutations.
result: For CSS codes with non-zero rate, one cannot address logical X, Z, H, or S gates to a strict subset of logical qubits using 1-local Clifford circuits. Also, permuting logical qubits by physical permutations is impossible if the rate exceeds 1/3 and distance is at least 3.
conclusion: The trade-off between addressability and code efficiency is fundamental, and this work provides new insights into the limitations of fault-tolerant operations on quantum codes.

title: Hierarchically Discriminating Haar-randomness In Quantum States From A Black-box Device
authors: Hao Wang And Adrián Pérez-Salinas Xavier Bonet-Monroig
abstract: The concept of randomness in quantum computing has been central to constructing benchmarking tools, cryptographic protocols, as well as a proof of beyond-classical computation. Discerning whether quantum states (or unitaries) are randomly distributed is a computational task that requires an enormous amount of quantum computational resources. This work addresses such a challenge by introducing a hierarchical discrimination algorithm to efficiently test if a set of states generated from a black-box quantum device with an unknown distribution is (in)compatible with a random distribution. To this end, we reduce the complexity of the problem by selecting an observable with known spectrum to study the statistical properties of its expectation values with respect to the quantum states from an unknown (black-box) quantum device. Concurrently, we use our first technical result, a connection between Haar-randomness and the Dirichlet distribution, to analytically compute Haar-random moments of the observable. Our Haar-random discriminator test is then simply to compare those statistical moments, such that if fails the test, it is enough to state that the quantum device does not output randomly distributed states. Else, we can not (yet) confirm that the states follow a Haar-random distribution. We further provide an extension to this algorithm by permutation- and unitary-equivalent randomization of the observable at increasing computational resources, which allows us to more accurately state whether is compatible with Haar-randomness. We envision the use of the discriminator test as a quantum device benchmark, by discriminating whether the states generated are incompatible with Haar-randomness.
tldr: This paper introduces a hierarchical algorithm to test whether quantum states from a black-box device are Haar-random, using statistical moments of observables.
motivation: Discerning Haar-randomness in quantum states is computationally hard but important for benchmarking and cryptographic protocols. The authors aim to reduce this complexity.
method: They select an observable with known spectrum, compute its expectation values over the unknown state distribution, and compare statistical moments to analytically derived Haar-random moments using a connection to the Dirichlet distribution. The algorithm can be extended with randomized observables.
result: The test can efficiently rule out Haar-randomness if moments mismatch, but cannot confirm randomness; it provides a hierarchical discrimination with increasing computational resources.
conclusion: The discriminator test serves as a practical benchmark for quantum devices, identifying non-random state distributions with limited resources.

title: Two-Way Wiretap Channel Under Mixed Secrecy Constraint
authors: Masahito Hayashi Yanling Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2607.20172v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies the two-way wiretap channel (TW-WC) with an external eavesdropper under strong one-sided (mixed) secrecy: only User~1's message is required to be secure from the eavesdropper, while no secrecy constraint is imposed on User~2's message. Secrecy is measured by the information leakage of User~1's message to the eavesdropper. Applying a non-adaptive construction and a one-sided reduction of the key-exchange construction, we obtain exponential error and leakage bounds for every fixed number of adaptive rounds. A quantitative one-time-pad argument propagates the leakage of the key used in the next round, and an explicit padding construction removes the initialization-rate loss for all sufficiently large blocklengths. We derive the corresponding strong mixed-secrecy achievable regions. The non-adaptive construction recovers the previously reported weak one-sided single-letter inner bound under the stronger secrecy criterion. The overall adaptive achievable region includes the non-adaptive construction as a fallback and also contains a key-exchange subregion that can be strictly larger.
tldr: This paper studies the two-way wiretap channel under a mixed secrecy constraint, deriving achievable secrecy regions with exponential error and leakage bounds.
motivation: To understand the fundamental limits of secure communication in two-way channels where only one user's message must be kept secret from an eavesdropper.
method: Uses non-adaptive and adaptive constructions with key exchange, a quantitative one-time-pad argument, and explicit padding to remove initialization-rate loss.
result: Obtains exponential error and leakage bounds for any fixed number of adaptive rounds, and derives strong mixed-secrecy achievable regions that include a key-exchange subregion potentially larger than the non-adaptive one.
conclusion: The adaptive construction can outperform non-adaptive schemes, and the results provide a comprehensive characterization of the two-way wiretap channel under mixed secrecy.

tldr: This paper studies entanglement dynamics in a system of two distinguishable particles with exchange interaction, revealing how exchange statistics affect entanglement generation and decay.
motivation: To understand the role of exchange statistics in entanglement dynamics of identical particles, which is often obscured by the interplay between exchange-induced correlations and the operational framework.

tldr: This paper develops an efficient classical surrogate for small subregions of quantum expectation landscapes, enabling hybrid quantum-classical simulation.
motivation: Classically simulating quantum circuits is generally hard, but for small patches of the landscape, efficient surrogates may be possible using initial quantum data.
method: The authors propose a method to classically surrogate a subregion of an expectation landscape by leveraging initial data from quantum computers, likely using techniques from classical shadow tomography or similar.

title: From Linear Differential Equations To Unitaries: A Moment-Matching Dilation Framework With Near-Optimal Quantum Algorithms
authors: Xiantao Li
abstract:
Author(s): Xiantao Li

[PRX Quantum 7, 020350] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: A moment-matching dilation framework maps nonunitary dynamics to a one-dimensional tight-binding lattice, enabling near-optimal quantum simulation of linear differential equations.
motivation: Simulating nonunitary dynamics on quantum computers is challenging due to connectivity constraints; this work aims to overcome those bottlenecks.
method: The authors develop a dilation approach that uses a one-dimensional tight-binding lattice as ancillary degrees of freedom, combined with moment-matching techniques to approximate the target nonunitary evolution.
result: The framework achieves near-optimal quantum algorithms for simulating linear differential equations, with improved resource scaling compared to previous methods.
conclusion: This work provides a practical and efficient method for quantum simulation of nonunitary processes, relevant to quantum information processing and quantum simulation.

title: Optimal Schedule Of Multi-channel Quantum Zeno Dragging With Application To Solving The k-SAT Problem
authors: Yipei Zhang, Alain Sarlette, Philippe Lewalle, Tathagata Karmakar, Thilo Scharnhorst, And K. Birgitta Whaley
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2167 (2026).

Quantum Zeno dragging enables the preparation of common eigenstates of a set of observables by frequent measurement and adiabatic-like modulation of the measurement basis. In this work, we present a deeper analysis of multi-channel Zeno dragging using generalized measurements, i.e. simultaneously measuring a set of non-commuting observables that vary slowly in time, to drag the state towards a target subspace. For concreteness, we will focus on a measurement-driven approach to solving k-SAT problems as examples. We first compute some analytical upper bounds on the convergence time, including the effect of finite measurement time resolution. We then apply optimal control theory to obtain the optimal dragging schedule that lower bounds the convergence time, for low-dimensional settings. This study provides a theoretical foundation for multi-channel Zeno dragging and its optimization, and also serves as a guide for designing optimal dragging schedules for quantum information tasks including measurement-driven quantum algorithms.

.
tldr: This paper analyzes multi-channel quantum Zeno dragging with generalized measurements and applies optimal control to schedule measurements for solving k-SAT problems.
motivation: Quantum Zeno dragging can prepare common eigenstates of observables, which is useful for measurement-driven quantum algorithms like solving k-SAT. The authors aim to optimize the dragging schedule to minimize convergence time.
method: The authors derive analytical upper bounds on convergence time, including finite measurement resolution effects, and apply optimal control theory to find the optimal dragging schedule in low-dimensional settings.
result: They obtain lower bounds on convergence time and demonstrate the optimal schedule for multi-channel Zeno dragging, providing a theoretical foundation for measurement-driven quantum algorithms.
conclusion: The work offers a guide for designing optimal dragging schedules for quantum information tasks, particularly measurement-driven quantum algorithms.

title: Steady-state Entanglement Harvesting For Two Rotating Atoms In A Cylindrical Cavity
authors: Hong-Tao Zheng, Xiang-Fa Zhou, Guang-Can Guo And Zheng-Wei Zhou
abstract: We study the entanglement dynamics of two rotating atoms (with two internal levels and ) in a cylindrical cavity, which interact with a massless scalar field in vacuum satisfying the Dirichlet boundary condition. Our analysis demonstrates that it is possible to obtain the steady-state entanglement under two types of resonant conditions. For two identical atoms with the same world-line, the system reduces to the usual dissipative Dicke model at the first resonant condition where and are the energy splitting and the angular velocity of the th atom, and is the Lorentz factor. The entangled steady-state takes the form where and are constant, which is consistent with the previous study (see 2022 Phys. Rev. D 106 105028). For two atoms with different world-lines, the system suffers from a significant mixed joint dissipation process at the second resonant condition , and reaches an entangled steady-state as . Moreover, with the help of the cavity, we can obtain a much higher concurrence in the final states by changing the relative ratio of the two orbital radii. Our work thus provides a more effective way for the extraction of steady-state entanglement from the vacuum via the analogue Unruh effect for two rotating atoms in a cylindrical cavity.
tldr: Two rotating atoms in a cylindrical cavity can harvest steady-state entanglement from the vacuum via the analogue Unruh effect, with cavity geometry enhancing concurrence.
motivation: To explore steady-state entanglement harvesting from vacuum using rotating atoms, which is relevant to quantum thermodynamics and information extraction.
method: The authors model two two-level atoms rotating in a cylindrical cavity with Dirichlet boundary conditions, interacting with a massless scalar field. They solve the master equation under two resonant conditions and compute concurrence.
result: Steady-state entanglement is achieved under two resonant conditions; for identical atoms it reduces to the Dicke model, while for different world-lines a mixed dissipation process occurs. Cavity geometry allows higher concurrence by tuning orbital radii.
conclusion: The work provides an effective method for extracting steady-state entanglement from vacuum using rotating atoms in a cavity, with potential applications in quantum information processing.

title: Machine-learned Syndrome Post-selection For Reliable Quantum Error Correction
authors: Tobias Haug, Askery Canabarro, Leandro Aolita
abstract: ArXiv:2607.19563v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum error correction can be enhanced by post-selecting out runs that are likely to produce a logical failure, but the most accurate measures for that require costly decoder-level information. We introduce a practical, decoder-agnostic post-selection method that learns directly from syndrome data. The method trains a supervised classifier to distinguish between syndromes from low- and high-noise regimes, and then uses the classifier's output as an abort score for new runs, without requiring logical-error labels, correction operators, or code-specific likelihood calculations. We validate the approach in three complementary settings: circuit-level simulations of the Gross bivariate-bicycle code, code-capacity simulations of the surface code, and experimental logical magic-state distillation data from the QuEra neutral-atom processor. In the Gross and surface codes, learned syndrome post-selection reduces the conditional logical error rate at a fixed acceptance rate, with performance comparable to syndrome-weight filtering. For the surface code, the learned classifier reveals a post-selection transition distinct from the conventional decoding threshold. In the experimental data, the machine-learning score outperforms syndrome-weight post-selection and, when combined with logical-gap filtering, improves the output fidelity beyond using the logical gap alone. These results show that syndrome-only learning provides a scalable and hardware-compatible route to improving the reliability of quantum error correction.
tldr: A machine learning method for post-selecting quantum error correction runs based solely on syndrome data, demonstrated on several codes and experimental data.
motivation: Post-selection can improve logical error rates but typically requires costly decoder-level information; the authors aim for a practical, decoder-agnostic approach.
method: Train a supervised classifier on syndrome data from low- and high-noise regimes to produce an abort score, without needing logical-error labels or correction operators.
result: The method reduces conditional logical error rates comparably to syndrome-weight filtering, reveals a post-selection transition in surface codes, and outperforms syndrome-weight filtering on experimental magic-state distillation data.
conclusion: Syndrome-only learning offers a scalable and hardware-compatible route to improving quantum error correction reliability.
